text: India produces over 60% of the world's vaccines, earning it the title 'pharmacy of the world.'
Traditional Chinese Medicine's pharmacopoeia includes over 12,000 substances — and Tu Youyou's malaria cure came directly from it.
Smallpox is the only human disease to have been completely eradicated — declared eliminated by WHO in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign.
Japan has the highest life expectancy in the world, averaging about 84 years — often attributed to diet, healthcare access, and social cohesion.
Cuba has a higher doctor-to-patient ratio than most wealthy nations and has produced globally significant lung cancer and meningitis vaccines.
The human gut microbiome contains roughly 38 trillion bacteria — slightly outnumbering human cells in the body.
Ayurveda, originating in India over 3,000 years ago, is one of the world's oldest holistic healing systems — 'ayur' means life, 'veda' means knowledge.
Rwanda achieved near-universal health coverage using community-based health insurance, reducing poverty-related deaths dramatically.
South Africa performed the world's first human heart transplant in 1967 — carried out by Dr. Christiaan Barnard at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when he noticed mold killing bacteria in a petri dish — it became the world's first widely used antibiotic.
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was first awarded in 1901 to Emil von Behring for his work on serum therapy against diphtheria.
The human body has 206 bones in adulthood, but babies are born with approximately 270 — many fuse together during childhood and adolescence.
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) was synthesized in 1897 by Felix Hoffmann at Bayer and remains one of the most widely consumed drugs in history.
MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) was developed from nuclear magnetic resonance research; Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield won the 2003 Nobel Prize for it.
Malaria kills over 600,000 people annually — more than 90% of deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, predominantly in children under five.
The first successful kidney transplant was performed by Joseph Murray in Boston in 1954 between identical twins; Murray later won the Nobel Prize in 1990.
Tuberculosis remains one of the world's top infectious killers, causing about 1.3 million deaths per year despite being largely preventable and treatable.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901; within a year X-ray imaging was used in surgery worldwide.
CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing technology, developed by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier, earned them the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and has opened new avenues for treating genetic diseases.
The polio vaccine developed by Jonas Salk in 1955 reduced polio cases in the United States by over 95% within just two years of its introduction.
The human heart beats approximately 100,000 times per day and pumps roughly 2,000 gallons of blood through about 60,000 miles of blood vessels.
Insulin was discovered in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto, transforming Type 1 diabetes from a death sentence into a manageable condition.
Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide, affecting over 280 million people; it is more common in women than in men.
The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, mapped all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA and identified approximately 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes.
Unani medicine, practiced widely across South Asia and the Middle East, traces its roots to ancient Greek physicians including Hippocrates and Galen.
Cholera killed tens of millions in seven global pandemics; John Snow's 1854 London investigation linking it to a contaminated water pump founded modern epidemiology.
The liver is the only internal organ capable of complete regeneration — it can regrow to its full size even after up to 75% has been removed.
The 1918 influenza pandemic infected an estimated 500 million people — one-third of the world's population — and killed at least 50 million.
Laparoscopic ('keyhole') surgery, introduced widely in the 1980s, allows surgeons to operate through tiny incisions using a camera, dramatically reducing recovery times.
Antibiotic resistance is projected to cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050 if left unchecked — surpassing cancer as a leading global killer.
Hippocrates of Cos, often called the 'Father of Medicine,' established medicine as a discipline distinct from religion around 400 BCE, introducing clinical observation.
The first prosthetic limb on record is an Egyptian wooden toe dated to around 950–710 BCE, found still attached to a mummy's foot.
Dengue fever infects an estimated 390 million people per year and is now endemic in over 100 countries, with cases rising as climate change expands mosquito habitats.
Telemedicine grew more than 3,800% during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since become a permanent fixture in healthcare delivery worldwide.
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy — a disease that killed more British sailors than combat before James Lind's 1747 trial showed citrus fruits as a cure.
The brain accounts for only 2% of body weight but consumes about 20% of the body's total energy and oxygen supply.
HIV/AIDS has killed over 40 million people since the epidemic began in the 1980s; antiretroviral therapy now allows people with HIV to live near-normal lifespans.
Ether was first used as a surgical anesthetic in 1846 by William Morton at Massachusetts General Hospital, ending the era of surgery without pain relief.
The BCG vaccine against tuberculosis, introduced in 1921, remains the most widely administered vaccine in history and is still recommended by WHO for infants.
Botulinum toxin (Botox), the most acutely toxic substance known, is used medically at extremely small doses to treat conditions ranging from migraines to muscle spasms.
Sickle cell disease, most prevalent in populations with ancestry from malaria-endemic regions, partially protects heterozygous carriers from severe malaria.
The first face transplant was performed in France in 2005 by surgeons Dubernard and Devauchelle, giving a patient severely mauled by a dog a new partial face.
Onchocerciasis (river blindness) affects about 21 million people; ivermectin donated by Merck has been a cornerstone of WHO's disease-elimination program since 1987.
The pancreas serves dual roles: as an exocrine gland secreting digestive enzymes and as an endocrine gland producing insulin and glucagon to regulate blood sugar.
Ethiopia's community health extension workers program, launched in 2003, trained over 40,000 workers and helped reduce child mortality by more than 50%.
The cornea is the only tissue in the human body without blood vessels; it receives oxygen directly from the surrounding air and tears.
Traditional African medicine is used by an estimated 80% of the African population as a primary or complementary form of healthcare.
Statins, first approved in 1987, are among the most prescribed drugs globally; they lower LDL cholesterol and have reduced cardiovascular mortality by millions per year.
Germ theory, established by Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch in the 19th century, proved that microorganisms cause infectious diseases and revolutionized medicine.
Sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis) is transmitted by the tsetse fly and was once nearly eliminated but resurged due to civil unrest disrupting control programs.
The number of neurons in the human brain is approximately 86 billion — roughly equivalent to the number of stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
Edward Jenner's 1796 cowpox vaccination against smallpox is considered the first vaccine ever developed, predating the germ theory of disease by nearly a century.
Robotic-assisted surgery, such as the da Vinci system approved by the FDA in 2000, enables surgeons to perform complex procedures with greater precision and smaller incisions.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) affects about 2–3% of the global population; it is classified by WHO among the top 10 most disabling illnesses.
Ambroise Paré, a 16th-century French barber-surgeon, pioneered the treatment of gunshot wounds and designed early prosthetic limbs, earning him the title 'Father of Surgery.'
The 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored Tu Youyou (artemisinin for malaria) and William Campbell and Satoshi Omura (ivermectin for parasitic diseases).
Nitrous oxide ('laughing gas') was first used as a dental anesthetic in 1844 by American dentist Horace Wells, who tested it on himself.
The retina contains about 120 million rod cells (for low-light vision) and 6 million cone cells (for color vision), packed into an area smaller than a postage stamp.
Bionic prosthetics with neural interfaces can now allow amputees to control robotic limbs through thought alone, using signals from residual nerves.
Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affect over 1.7 billion people in low-income countries; many are preventable with cheap interventions but receive less than 1% of global health funding.
The appendix was long considered vestigial, but research now suggests it may serve as a reservoir of beneficial gut bacteria after intestinal infections.
Siddha medicine, one of India's oldest medical systems, originated in Tamil Nadu and uses minerals, metals, and herbs — with written texts dating back over 2,000 years.
Organ donation rates vary enormously by country: Spain has one of the highest opt-out systems and consistently leads the world in deceased donor transplants per million.
Schizophrenia affects approximately 24 million people worldwide; it is highly heritable but also influenced by environmental triggers including cannabis use.
The diaphragm is the primary muscle of respiration; a hiccup is an involuntary spasm of the diaphragm causing the glottis to snap shut, producing the characteristic sound.
Bone marrow transplantation, first successful in 1968, can cure many blood cancers and disorders by replacing diseased marrow with healthy donor stem cells.
The World Health Organization was founded in 1948 and its first act was addressing malaria; it is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.
Lithium has been used since 1949 to treat bipolar disorder and remains one of the most effective mood-stabilizing medications, though its exact mechanism is still not fully understood.
Guinea worm disease (dracunculiasis) has been reduced from 3.5 million cases in 1986 to just a handful annually — largely through the work of the Carter Center without a vaccine or drug.
The spleen filters blood, removing old red blood cells and pathogens; people without a spleen must take prophylactic antibiotics for life due to increased infection risk.
The placebo effect — where patients improve due to belief in treatment — is so powerful it has measurable physiological effects, including releasing endogenous opioids.
Ignaz Semmelweis demonstrated in 1847 that handwashing by doctors reduced puerperal fever deaths in maternity wards — yet was ridiculed and dismissed by the medical establishment.
Blood typing was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901, allowing safe blood transfusions and earning him the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1930.
Nearly half of the world's population — about 3.5 billion people — is at risk of malaria, with sub-Saharan Africa bearing more than 90% of global cases.
The cochlear implant, first implanted in 1961, converts sound to electrical signals delivered directly to the auditory nerve, restoring hearing in profoundly deaf patients.
Artemisinin, derived from sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua) and used in Chinese medicine for 2,000 years, is now a frontline malaria treatment recommended by WHO.
The thymus gland trains T-cells of the immune system during childhood; it gradually shrinks after puberty and is largely replaced by fat by old age.
The global obesity epidemic has tripled since 1975; today more than 1 billion adults are obese, increasing risks of diabetes, heart disease, and certain cancers.
Photodynamic therapy uses light-activated drugs to kill cancer cells and has been approved for treating certain lung, esophageal, and skin cancers.
Radiation therapy for cancer was first used in 1896, just one year after Röntgen discovered X-rays; today it is used in about half of all cancer treatments.
Chagas disease, endemic to Latin America, is caused by a parasite transmitted by 'kissing bugs' and can cause fatal heart disease decades after initial infection.
The WHO's DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course) strategy for tuberculosis has saved an estimated 76 million lives since its launch in 1995.
More than 2 billion people in the world are infected with the bacteria that cause tuberculosis, though only about 5–10% develop active disease in their lifetime.
CAR-T cell therapy, approved by the FDA in 2017, engineers a patient's own immune cells to attack cancer and has produced remarkable remissions in some blood cancers.
Florence Nightingale revolutionized nursing and hospital sanitation during the Crimean War (1853–1856), reducing mortality in field hospitals from 42% to just 2%.
The pituitary gland, no larger than a pea, is the 'master gland' of the endocrine system, producing hormones that regulate growth, reproduction, and other gland functions.
Artemisinin combination therapy (ACT) reduced malaria deaths by over 50% globally between 2000 and 2015, one of the greatest public health successes of the era.
The first mRNA vaccines — for COVID-19 from Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna — were developed and authorized in under a year, the fastest vaccine development in history.
Doctors Without Borders (Médecins Sans Frontières), founded in 1971, has provided emergency medical care in over 70 countries and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999.
The lymphatic system, often overlooked, is critical for immune defense and fluid balance — lymph nodes swell during infection as they filter out pathogens.
Global tobacco use kills over 8 million people per year; smoking is the leading preventable cause of death worldwide, causing cancer, heart disease, and stroke.
The first recorded cesarean section on a living patient (with the mother surviving) took place in 1500 in Switzerland, performed by Jakob Nufer on his own wife.
The 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for discoveries enabling mRNA vaccine development.
Lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) affects over 51 million people; mass drug administration programs have reduced new infections by over 74% since 2000.
Naloxone (Narcan) can reverse an opioid overdose within minutes; it is now available without prescription in many countries to combat the opioid crisis.
Tai chi, rooted in traditional Chinese martial arts and medicine, has been shown in randomized trials to reduce falls in older adults by up to 50%.
The first successful lung transplant was performed by Joel Cooper in Toronto in 1983; double-lung transplants followed in 1986.
Water fluoridation, introduced in the US in 1945, is recognized by the CDC as one of the 10 great public health achievements of the 20th century for reducing tooth decay.
Acupuncture, a cornerstone of Traditional Chinese Medicine practiced for over 2,000 years, has been shown in meta-analyses to modestly reduce chronic pain.
The global burden of cardiovascular disease kills 17.9 million people annually — roughly one-third of all deaths worldwide.
Watson and Crick's 1953 discovery of the DNA double helix, informed by Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data, earned Watson, Crick, and Wilkins the Nobel Prize in 1962.
Photoplethysmography — the technology behind pulse oximeters — was commercialized in the 1980s and became standard care; its racial bias in darker skin tones is now a recognized clinical issue.
The placenta is a temporary organ unique to pregnancy; it produces hormones, exchanges nutrients and waste, and acts as an immune barrier between mother and fetus.
Gene therapy delivered a functional gene to a child with ADA-SCID ('bubble boy disease') in 1990, marking the first approved human gene therapy trial.
The Ebola virus, first identified in 1976 near the Ebola River in DR Congo, has caused multiple deadly outbreaks; the 2014–2016 West Africa epidemic infected over 28,000 people.
Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia, affects over 55 million people worldwide; lecanemab became the first FDA-approved drug to slow its progression in 2023.
Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) — a simple mix of water, sugar, and salt — is credited with saving over 50 million lives since its introduction in the 1970s.
Leeches, once a cornerstone of medieval bloodletting, are today FDA-approved medical devices used to restore circulation in reattachment surgery.
Maggot therapy (using sterile fly larvae to clean wounds) has been shown in clinical trials to debride chronic wounds faster than conventional surgery.
The first 3D-printed organ scaffolds were implanted experimentally in the 2010s; researchers successfully 3D-printed a functional human heart scaffold in 2019.
Zoonotic diseases — those that jump from animals to humans — account for 60% of all infectious diseases; over 70% of emerging pathogens originate in wildlife.
GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) were developed for diabetes but have proven so effective for weight loss they have reshaped obesity treatment.
The pineal gland produces melatonin in response to darkness, regulating circadian rhythms; René Descartes once called it the 'seat of the soul.'
The first pacemaker implant was performed in 1958 in Sweden by surgeon Åke Senning; today over 1 million pacemakers are implanted worldwide annually.
Trachoma, a bacterial eye infection, is the world's leading infectious cause of blindness; it is transmitted by flies and touch, and disproportionately affects women and children.
Corticosteroids, discovered in the 1940s, revolutionized treatment of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases; Philip Hench and Edward Kendall won the 1950 Nobel Prize for cortisone.
The vagus nerve is the longest cranial nerve, running from the brain through the chest and abdomen; it regulates heart rate, digestion, and is central to the 'gut-brain axis.'
The Mütter Museum in Philadelphia houses thousands of medical specimens including the conjoined liver of Chang and Eng Bunker, the original 'Siamese twins.'
The first separation of conjoined twins was recorded in 1689; modern surgical separation has a high success rate when twins do not share a heart.
Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has transformed emergency medicine and is now used in low-income countries on smartphones and portable devices costing a few hundred dollars.
Hunger and malnutrition remain major global health challenges — about 2.8 billion people cannot afford a healthy diet, with consequences spanning stunting to micronutrient deficiencies.
Sulfonamides, the first synthetic antibacterials, were developed by Gerhard Domagk in 1932; they saved countless lives in WWII and paved the way for modern antibiotics.
Polio has been eliminated from all countries except Afghanistan and Pakistan, where the wild virus still circulates as of 2024.
Therapeutic hypothermia — cooling the body to around 33°C after cardiac arrest — reduces brain injury and was introduced as standard care in the early 2000s.
Avicenna (Ibn Sina), an 11th-century Persian physician, wrote the 'Canon of Medicine' — a medical encyclopedia that was used in European universities until the 17th century.
The human kidney filters approximately 200 liters of blood every day, producing about 1–2 liters of urine while reclaiming water, salts, and nutrients.
Liquid biopsies — detecting tumor DNA circulating in blood — are a rapidly advancing diagnostic tool that could allow earlier cancer detection without invasive biopsies.
Dopamine, a neurotransmitter often called the 'reward chemical,' plays a critical role in motivation, movement, and emotional responses; its depletion causes Parkinson's disease.
The Zika virus, discovered in Uganda in 1947, caused a major epidemic in the Americas in 2015–2016; its link to microcephaly in newborns was confirmed by the WHO in 2016.
Percutaneous coronary intervention (balloon angioplasty), first performed by Andreas Grüntzig in 1977, became one of the most common procedures for treating heart attacks.
The human immune system has two main branches: innate immunity (fast, non-specific) and adaptive immunity (slower but highly specific and long-lasting).
Ethiopia, Bolivia, and Nepal have dramatically reduced maternal mortality through task-shifting — allowing trained midwives and nurses to perform duties formerly restricted to doctors.
Stem cell therapy holds promise for conditions from spinal injury to Parkinson's; the first approved stem cell treatment was bone marrow transplantation used for leukemia.
Serotonin syndrome, caused by too much serotonergic activity, can be triggered by combining certain antidepressants and is a potentially life-threatening emergency.
In 2020, WHO listed burnout as an occupational phenomenon with three dimensions: exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced professional efficacy.
The discovery that H. pylori bacteria — not stress — causes most peptic ulcers earned Barry Marshall and Robin Warren the 2005 Nobel Prize; Marshall proved it by infecting himself.
Kangaroo mother care — keeping preterm newborns in continuous skin-to-skin contact with a parent — reduces neonatal mortality by over 40% and originated in Bogotá, Colombia.
The first CT scanner was developed by Godfrey Hounsfield and demonstrated in 1971; he shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the invention.
The measles vaccine has saved over 56 million lives since 1980; yet vaccination coverage gaps caused measles cases to rebound to 9.7 million globally in 2023.
Pharmacogenomics studies how genes affect a person's response to drugs; variants in CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 enzymes affect metabolism of dozens of common medications.
The Affordable Care Act in the US (2010) extended health coverage to over 20 million people; it remains a major case study in public health policy worldwide.
PET scans (Positron Emission Tomography) use radioactive tracers to visualize metabolic activity; they are invaluable for diagnosing cancer and neurological diseases.
The 1918 influenza disproportionately killed young adults aged 20–40 — an unusual pattern possibly caused by immune overreaction (cytokine storm) in those with stronger immune systems.
Xenotransplantation — transplanting organs from genetically modified pigs into humans — achieved a milestone when a pig kidney functioned in a human for 47 days in 2023.
Magnesium sulfate, an inexpensive mineral compound, is WHO's recommended treatment for eclampsia in pregnancy — preventing seizures and saving thousands of mothers' lives annually.
The human eye can distinguish approximately 10 million different colors — but only has three types of cone cells, each responding to different wavelengths of light.
Chronic kidney disease affects about 850 million people globally — more than diabetes and cancer combined — and is the fastest-growing cause of death worldwide.
Yoga, documented in the Rigveda (c. 1500 BCE) and central to Ayurvedic wellness, has been shown to reduce blood pressure, anxiety, and chronic pain in clinical trials.
Epidural anesthesia, now standard in labor and many surgeries, was first developed by Fidel Pagés in Spain in 1921 but popularized later by John Cleland in the US.
Noma (cancrum oris) is a rapidly destructive disease of the face mostly affecting malnourished children in sub-Saharan Africa; WHO added it to the neglected tropical diseases list in 2023.
The first synthetic opioid, meperidine (Demerol), was synthesized in 1939 while researching anticholinergic compounds — its opioid properties were discovered by accident.
In Mexico and Central America, traditional healers called 'curanderos' integrate herbal medicine, spiritual healing, and community rituals into healthcare still widely used today.
Psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy using psilocybin has shown remarkable results in Phase 2 clinical trials for treatment-resistant depression, with effects lasting months after one or two sessions.
Anemia affects over 1.6 billion people globally — the most common nutritional disorder — with iron-deficiency anemia accounting for the largest share.
The spinal cord houses the central pattern generators for walking, meaning the legs can produce rhythmic stepping movements without direct input from the brain.
Andrew Taylor Still founded osteopathic medicine in 1874, emphasizing the relationship between the musculoskeletal system and overall health; today 25% of US doctors hold a DO degree.
Lyme disease, spread by tick bites, was first described in 1975 in Old Lyme, Connecticut; it is now the most common vector-borne disease in the Northern Hemisphere.
Cardiac stents — mesh tubes inserted to keep coronary arteries open — were first implanted in humans in 1986 and are now placed in millions of patients annually worldwide.
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) declines with aging; research into NAD+ precursors as potential anti-aging interventions is ongoing in multiple Phase 2 trials.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgical techniques using carbolic acid in 1865, reducing postoperative mortality dramatically and founding modern surgical asepsis.
Long COVID affects an estimated 10–20% of those infected with SARS-CoV-2, with symptoms including fatigue, brain fog, and shortness of breath persisting for months or years.
The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak in London, investigated by John Snow, is considered the founding moment of modern epidemiology and disease mapping.
Traditional Tibetan medicine (Sowa Rigpa) is an ancient system integrating Ayurveda and Chinese medicine; it uses pulse diagnosis and herbal preparations and is practiced across the Himalayas.
The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body; it drains lymph from the entire body except the right upper quadrant and empties into the left subclavian vein.
Intermittent fasting regimens have been shown in randomized trials to reduce blood pressure, improve insulin sensitivity, and reduce inflammatory markers.
Monkeypox (mpox) was first identified in laboratory monkeys in 1958 and in humans in 1970; the 2022 global outbreak prompted WHO to declare it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.
The 2010 Haiti earthquake killed over 220,000 people; the resulting cholera epidemic — inadvertently introduced by UN peacekeepers — killed a further 10,000 in the following years.
The appendicular skeleton — arms, legs, shoulder girdles, and pelvis — has 126 bones, while the axial skeleton comprising the skull, spine, and rib cage has 80.
Marburg virus, closely related to Ebola, was first identified in 1967 in laboratory workers in Marburg, Germany exposed to infected African green monkeys.
The Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015) reduced under-five child mortality globally by more than half, largely through vaccines, nutrition programs, and basic healthcare access.
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2024 was awarded to Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun for their discovery of microRNA, small RNA molecules that regulate gene expression.
Breastfeeding for the first six months of life reduces infant mortality from diarrhea by 11 times and from respiratory infections by four times, according to WHO.
Fetal surgery to correct spina bifida in the womb, pioneered at the University of California San Francisco, significantly improves neurological outcomes compared to postnatal repair.
Meningococcal meningitis sweeps sub-Saharan Africa's 'meningitis belt' in seasonal epidemics; MenAfriVac, a $0.50 vaccine developed for Africa, has nearly eliminated meningitis A from the region.
Nanotechnology in medicine includes nanoparticle drug delivery systems that can target tumors directly, reducing the side effects of chemotherapy.
Vietnam dramatically reduced malaria deaths by 97% between 1991 and 1997 using community-based early diagnosis and artemisinin treatment — a model replicated worldwide.
Circadian medicine — timing drug administration to match the body's biological clock — has been shown to improve efficacy and reduce toxicity of cancer chemotherapy.
The adrenal glands, sitting atop each kidney, produce over 50 hormones including adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol, which drive the fight-or-flight stress response.
The first use of anesthetic in childbirth was by James Young Simpson in 1847 using chloroform, but it was controversial until Queen Victoria used it for her eighth delivery in 1853.
The Japanese practice of 'shinrin-yoku' (forest bathing) has been studied in randomized trials showing reductions in cortisol, blood pressure, and heart rate.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is an FDA-approved, non-invasive treatment for treatment-resistant depression that uses magnetic pulses to stimulate nerve cells in the brain.
Roughly 12% of adults worldwide — about 900 million people — have prediabetes, putting them at high risk of developing Type 2 diabetes, which is largely preventable with lifestyle changes.
The global surgery crisis: 5 billion people lack access to safe, affordable surgical care; 143 million additional procedures are needed annually to address the unmet burden.
Diphtheria, once a leading killer of children, has been reduced by 90% worldwide through vaccination; the DTP vaccine is one of WHO's core immunization recommendations.
Andrew Weil popularized 'integrative medicine' — combining evidence-based conventional care with complementary approaches — and co-founded the Arizona Center for Integrative Medicine in 1994.
The fascia — sheets of connective tissue surrounding muscles and organs — is now recognized as a mechanosensory organ involved in proprioception and chronic pain.
PEPFAR (US President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief), launched in 2003, is the largest commitment by any nation to address a single disease — it has supported over 20 million on HIV treatment.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS), implanting electrodes to deliver electrical impulses to targeted brain regions, provides remarkable relief for Parkinson's symptoms in candidates who don't respond to medication.
Herceptin (trastuzumab), the first targeted cancer therapy based on a tumor's genetic profile, was approved in 1998 for HER2-positive breast cancer and transformed oncology.
The retrovirus HTLV-1 is the only known human retrovirus aside from HIV; it causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and is endemic in Japan, the Caribbean, and parts of Africa.
Global handwashing with soap could prevent roughly 1 million deaths annually; yet as of 2023, about 2 billion people still lack access to a basic handwashing facility at home.
The longest surgery on record lasted 103 hours in 1951 in Chicago, when Dr. Gertrude Levandowski removed a 303-pound ovarian cyst.
Kinesio tape, developed by Japanese chiropractor Kenzo Kase in 1973, gained global visibility at the 2008 Olympics and has modest evidence for pain reduction in certain conditions.
The blood-brain barrier, formed by tight junctions in brain capillaries, protects the brain from pathogens and toxins but also makes drug delivery to the brain extremely challenging.
Leprosy (Hansen's disease), caused by Mycobacterium leprae, has been curable since the 1980s with multidrug therapy; yet stigma keeps over 200,000 new cases from seeking care each year.
Artificial intelligence models have matched or exceeded dermatologists in detecting melanoma from photographs in multiple published studies, pointing toward AI as a diagnostic tool.
The BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations significantly increase lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer; testing for them — made famous by Angelina Jolie in 2013 — has saved many lives.
The eye's aqueous humor is continuously produced and drained; when drainage is impaired it raises intraocular pressure, causing glaucoma — the second leading cause of blindness globally.
Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) — transferring stool from a healthy donor — cures recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection in about 90% of cases, outperforming antibiotics.
Sudan and South Sudan have the world's highest burden of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar); without treatment this parasitic disease is nearly always fatal.
Wearable continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), now available without prescription in many countries, allow diabetics to track blood sugar in real time, reducing hypoglycemic episodes significantly.
The thyroid gland, shaped like a butterfly at the base of the neck, produces hormones regulating metabolism, heart rate, and temperature; hypothyroidism affects 5% of adults globally.
Blood doping — transfusing extra red blood cells or using EPO — was endemic in professional cycling in the 1990s; it increases oxygen-carrying capacity by up to 10%.
Preventive chemotherapy — giving entire communities scheduled antiparasitic drugs regardless of individual infection status — is WHO's primary strategy against NTDs in high-risk populations.
The gut-brain axis — the bidirectional communication network between the enteric nervous system and the central nervous system — may explain why gut bacteria influence mood and anxiety.
In 2023, Casgevy became the first CRISPR-based therapy approved by the FDA and MHRA — it functionally cures sickle cell disease by reactivating fetal hemoglobin.
Clean cooking fuel access is a major global health issue: indoor air pollution from burning solid fuels causes 3.2 million deaths per year — more than HIV/AIDS.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors such as ipilimumab and pembrolizumab remove brakes on the immune system to attack cancer; James Allison and Tasuku Honjo won the 2018 Nobel Prize for this discovery.
Universal health coverage — ensuring all people can access quality health services without financial hardship — is enshrined in the UN Sustainable Development Goals as a target to be reached by 2030.

Progeria (Hutchinson–Gilford syndrome) is an ultra-rare accelerated aging disorder caused by a point mutation in the LMNA gene; affected children typically die of cardiovascular disease in their early teens.

The Orphan Drug Act of 1983 in the United States incentivized pharmaceutical companies to develop treatments for rare diseases affecting fewer than 200,000 Americans, leading to over 600 approved orphan drugs by 2020.
Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and eyes; the characteristic Kayser–Fleischer ring in the cornea is a clinical hallmark.

CT (computed tomography) scanning, invented by Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack, earned them the 1979 Nobel Prize; the technology takes hundreds of X-ray images from different angles to construct 3D cross-sections.

MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) was developed in the 1970s by Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield, who shared the 2003 Nobel Prize; it uses powerful magnetic fields and radio waves rather than ionizing radiation.

PET (positron emission tomography) scans detect metabolic activity in tissues by tracking radioactive tracers; they are critical in oncology for identifying cancer spread and in neurology for diagnosing Alzheimer's.
Harvey Cushing, the father of modern neurosurgery, pioneered techniques for operating on brain tumors in the early 20th century and reduced surgical mortality from over 90% to under 10%.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS), FDA-approved in 1997 for essential tremor and Parkinson's disease, involves implanting electrodes in specific brain regions to modulate abnormal neural circuits with electrical pulses.

The first successful human kidney transplant was performed in 1954 by Joseph Murray in Boston between identical twins; Murray later received the Nobel Prize in 1990 for his work on organ transplantation.
The first successful liver transplant was performed in 1967 by Thomas Starzl in Pittsburgh; cyclosporine, discovered in 1976, dramatically improved survival by preventing organ rejection.
Christiaan Barnard performed the world's first human-to-human heart transplant in Cape Town, South Africa in 1967; the patient, Louis Washkansky, survived 18 days.

The first successful blood transfusion in humans using the ABO compatibility system was performed by Reuben Ottenberg in 1907; Karl Landsteiner had discovered ABO blood groups in 1901, earning him the 1930 Nobel Prize.
Blood banking was made possible by the discovery that adding sodium citrate prevented clotting and that refrigeration preserved blood; the first blood bank opened in Leningrad in 1932.

Diethyl ether was first used as a surgical anesthetic in 1846 by William Morton at Massachusetts General Hospital; the event is often called the 'ether day' and transformed surgery from an agonizing ordeal.
Chloroform was popularized as an anesthetic in the 1840s by James Young Simpson; Queen Victoria used it during childbirth in 1853, helping legitimize anesthesia for obstetrics.
Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery in 1867 using carbolic acid (phenol) sprays based on Pasteur's germ theory, dramatically reducing post-surgical infections and mortality.

Ignaz Semmelweis discovered in 1847 that handwashing with chlorinated lime reduced puerperal fever mortality from 18% to under 2% in his Vienna maternity ward, yet his findings were ridiculed and rejected for decades.
The placebo effect — improvement in a patient's condition due to belief in a treatment rather than the treatment itself — can produce measurable physiological changes including endorphin release.

Open-label placebos — where patients know they are taking a sugar pill — still produce clinically significant improvements in irritable bowel syndrome and chronic back pain, challenging simplistic explanations of placebo.
The Declaration of Helsinki (1964) established ethical principles for medical research on human subjects, including the requirement for informed consent and favorable risk-benefit assessment.

The Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972) withheld penicillin treatment from 399 Black American men to study untreated syphilis; its exposure led to sweeping reforms in research ethics and the 1979 Belmont Report.

The Nuremberg Code (1947), drawn up after Nazi medical experiments, established that voluntary informed consent is absolutely essential in any human experiment — forming the cornerstone of modern research ethics.

The first randomized controlled trial (RCT) in medicine was conducted in 1948 by Austin Bradford Hill, testing streptomycin for tuberculosis; the RCT became the gold standard for evaluating medical interventions.

The RECOVERY trial (2020) used a streamlined adaptive design to test multiple COVID-19 treatments simultaneously, discovering that cheap dexamethasone reduced deaths in severely ill patients by one third.

The Global Health Security Index assesses pandemic preparedness across 195 countries; the 2021 report found that no country was fully prepared, and high-income countries did not necessarily perform best.

The International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) legally bind 196 countries to report and respond to public health events of international concern, creating the framework for the WHO to declare Public Health Emergencies.
The One Health concept recognizes that human, animal, and environmental health are interconnected and interdependent; approximately 60% of known human infectious diseases originated in animals.

Nipah virus, first identified in Malaysia in 1998, jumped from fruit bats to pigs to humans; its case fatality rate can exceed 70%, and it has caused repeated outbreaks in Bangladesh and India with no approved vaccine.

SARS-CoV-1 (2002–2003) originated in horseshoe bats and spread via palm civets to humans in Guangdong, China; the outbreak infected 8,098 people and killed 774 before being contained by public health measures.

Google DeepMind's AI system AlphaFold2 (2020) predicted the 3D structure of nearly every known protein with atomic accuracy, solving a 50-year-old grand challenge in biology with enormous implications for drug discovery.
AI systems trained on retinal photographs can now predict cardiovascular risk factors — including age, sex, blood pressure, and smoking status — that are not normally visible to the human eye.
The FDA approved the first AI-based medical imaging diagnostic tool in 2018 — IDx-DR, which autonomously detects diabetic retinopathy from retinal photographs without a physician's immediate review.

Liposomal drug delivery, used in treatments like Doxil (liposomal doxorubicin), encapsulates chemotherapy drugs in lipid nanoparticles to improve tumor targeting and reduce toxicity to healthy tissue.

Iron oxide nanoparticles approved for MRI contrast (ferumoxytol) and iron deficiency treatment can also be engineered to destroy tumors via magnetic hyperthermia, heating only cancer cells when exposed to alternating magnetic fields.

CAR-T (chimeric antigen receptor T-cell) therapy engineers a patient's own T cells to express receptors targeting cancer cells; Kymriah (tisagenlecleucel) became the first FDA-approved CAR-T therapy in 2017 for B-cell leukemia.

CAR-T therapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma achieves complete remission in approximately 40% of patients who had failed all other treatments, representing a major breakthrough for otherwise incurable blood cancers.

The cochlear implant, invented by Graeme Clark in Australia in the 1970s and first commercially implanted in 1982, bypasses damaged hair cells in the inner ear by directly stimulating the auditory nerve with electrical signals.

Over 700,000 people worldwide have received cochlear implants; in congenitally deaf children implanted before age 3, outcomes for speech and language development are nearly equivalent to hearing peers.

The Argus II retinal implant (2013), also called a bionic eye, converts video from a wearable camera into electrical pulses that stimulate residual retinal cells, allowing some blind patients to perceive shapes and movement.
CRISPR-Cas9 was awarded the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier; the technology uses RNA-guided nucleases to edit DNA with unprecedented precision.

The first approved CRISPR therapy, Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), targets the BCL11A enhancer to reactivate gamma-globin production, effectively curing both sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia.

Gaucher disease, the most common lysosomal storage disorder, is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase; enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with imiglucerase transformed it from a fatal disease to a manageable one.

Pompe disease, a rare glycogen storage disorder, was the first lysosomal storage disease treated with a recombinant enzyme — alglucosidase alfa (Myozyme), approved by the FDA in 2006 and hailed as a landmark for rare disease treatment.

Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 1, once invariably fatal in infancy, was transformed by nusinersen (Spinraza) in 2016 and then by the gene therapy onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) in 2019 — at $2.1 million the most expensive drug ever at launch.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) was the first genetic disease screened for in newborns, starting in the early 1960s; universal newborn screening now prevents intellectual disability that would otherwise result from phenylalanine accumulation.

X-ray crystallography, used by Rosalind Franklin to produce Photo 51 in 1952, provided crucial evidence for the double-helix structure of DNA; Watson and Crick used this data without Franklin's full knowledge.

Fluoroscopy allows real-time continuous X-ray imaging; it is used in cardiac catheterizations, orthopedic procedures, and swallowing studies but exposes patients to significantly more radiation than standard X-rays.

Functional MRI (fMRI) measures blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals to map brain activity; it transformed neuroscience by allowing researchers to observe which brain regions activate during specific tasks.

The stereotactic radiosurgery system Gamma Knife, developed by Lars Leksell in 1968, delivers focused beams of gamma radiation to brain tumors with submillimeter precision, treating conditions inoperable by conventional surgery.

Walter Dandy, a pioneer of neurosurgery at Johns Hopkins in the 1910s–1930s, developed ventriculography (injecting air into the brain's ventricles for imaging), performed the first hemispherectomy, and clipped the first cerebral aneurysm.

The bionic hand i-Limb, first marketed in 2007, was the world's first commercially available prosthetic hand with individually powered fingers and a rotating thumb, restoring grip patterns for upper limb amputees.

Targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR) surgery reroutes nerves from an amputated limb to nearby muscle groups, creating new nerve signals that can be read by advanced prosthetics to enable more intuitive limb control.
Osseointegrated prosthetics anchor directly to the bone via a titanium implant, eliminating socket discomfort and dramatically improving proprioception and mobility for above-knee amputees.

Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) affects approximately 1 in 250 people worldwide and dramatically increases early cardiovascular disease risk; it is severely underdiagnosed, with only 10% of cases identified globally.

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) causes abnormal blood vessel formations (arteriovenous malformations) throughout the body; it affects 1 in 5,000 people and can cause strokes, pulmonary hemorrhage, and liver complications.

Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune neurological disorder causing progressive muscle rigidity and painful spasms; singer Celine Dion publicly disclosed her diagnosis in 2022, raising awareness of the condition.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common infectious cause of birth defects in the developed world, affecting 1 in 200 newborns; congenital CMV can cause hearing loss, vision problems, and intellectual disabilities.

Brucellosis, caused by the bacterial genus Brucella, is the most widespread zoonosis globally; transmitted through unpasteurized dairy products and contact with infected animals, it can cause chronic debilitating illness.

Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii bacteria, is a zoonosis transmitted via inhalation of contaminated particles from infected livestock; a 2007–2011 Dutch outbreak infected over 4,000 people and led to mass goat vaccinations.

CEPI (Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations), founded in 2017, aims to develop vaccines against priority pathogens within 100 days of identifying a new pandemic threat, a goal accelerated by COVID-19 experience.

Pandemic influenza preparedness stockpiles H5N1 vaccines in strategic national reserves; the 1918 Spanish flu, caused by an H1N1 strain, infected 500 million and killed 50–100 million — the deadliest pandemic in recorded history.

Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are laboratory-produced proteins that mimic immune system antibodies and can be designed to bind specific targets; the first approved mAb, muromonab-CD3 (OKT3), was used in 1986 to prevent organ rejection.

Trastuzumab (Herceptin), approved in 1998, targets HER2-positive breast cancer cells and was the first targeted cancer therapy based on tumor genetic profiling, transforming outcomes for a previously aggressive breast cancer subtype.

Bispecific antibodies can simultaneously bind two different antigens — for example, blinatumomab (Blincyto) bridges CD3 on T cells and CD19 on leukemia cells, recruiting immune cells directly to kill cancer.

Tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy extracts immune cells from a patient's own tumor, expands them billions-fold in the lab, and reinfuses them; in 2024 lifileucel became the first FDA-approved TIL therapy for melanoma.

mRNA vaccines work by instructing cells to produce a viral protein, triggering an immune response; prior to COVID-19, Katalin Karikó spent decades refining the technology — often without institutional support — enabling the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine.

The Salk polio vaccine (1955) was among the first large-scale double-blind controlled trials in history, involving 1.8 million children; Jonas Salk famously declined to patent it, saying 'the people' owned the vaccine.

Variolation — deliberately infecting people with material from smallpox pustules — was practiced in China and the Ottoman Empire centuries before Jenner's cowpox vaccine, with mortality of around 2% compared to 30% from natural smallpox.

The Ebola vaccine rVSV-ZEBOV (Ervebo), approved in 2019 by the FDA and EMA, was evaluated in a ring vaccination strategy during the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak, providing approximately 100% efficacy in its trial.

Malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum kills approximately 600,000 people annually; the RTS,S/AS01 vaccine (Mosquirix), approved by WHO in 2021, is the first licensed vaccine against a parasitic disease.

The nocebo effect — experiencing adverse symptoms in response to a placebo due to negative expectations — is responsible for a significant proportion of reported side effects in clinical trials and can be severe enough to cause death.

Adaptive clinical trial designs allow modifications to the trial — such as stopping early for efficacy or futility — based on accumulated data, reducing exposure to ineffective treatments and speeding regulatory approval.

Platform trials like I-SPY 2 for breast cancer run multiple experimental drugs simultaneously against a common control, using Bayesian adaptive designs to graduate promising agents to phase 3 much faster than traditional methods.

Waddell's signs, described in 1980, are five clinical tests used to identify non-organic (psychological) components in low back pain; they are controversial but highlight the importance of psychological factors in chronic pain.

Onchocerciasis (river blindness), caused by a parasitic worm spread by blackflies near fast-flowing rivers, has been nearly eliminated in West Africa through the African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control using ivermectin.

GPCR (G protein-coupled receptor) drugs account for approximately 34% of all FDA-approved medications, including beta-blockers, antihistamines, and opioids; Robert Lefkowitz and Brian Kobilka won the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for GPCR structure.

Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are short synthetic DNA strands that bind complementary mRNA sequences to block or alter gene expression; nusinersen (Spinraza) for SMA was among the first successful ASO drugs.

RNA interference (RNAi) silences genes using small interfering RNA (siRNA); inclisiran, a siRNA approved in 2020, silences the PCSK9 gene in the liver with a twice-yearly injection, dramatically reducing LDL cholesterol.

Phage therapy — using bacteriophage viruses to kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria — was practiced in Eastern Europe throughout the 20th century; it is now experiencing a global renaissance as antimicrobial resistance worsens.

The ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter species) are the leading cause of hospital-acquired infections and are resistant to most antibiotics.

The first lung transplant was performed in 1963 by James Hardy in Mississippi; the patient survived 18 days. The first successful long-term lung transplant was carried out by Joel Cooper in Toronto in 1983.
Uterus transplants, first reported as a live-birth success in Sweden in 2014 by Mats Brannstrom's team, have since enabled dozens of women with absolute uterine infertility to carry pregnancies.

The first face transplant was performed in France in 2005 by Bernard Devauchelle and Jean-Michel Dubernard on Isabelle Dinoire, who had been mauled by a dog; the partial transplant restored lip and nose function.

Xenotransplantation — transplanting animal organs into humans — advanced significantly in 2022 when surgeons at the University of Maryland transplanted a genetically modified pig heart into a living patient; he survived 60 days.
POEMS syndrome is an ultra-rare blood disorder caused by an abnormal plasma cell clone; the acronym stands for Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M-protein, and Skin changes.

Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), the rarest disabling condition known, causes muscle and connective tissue to slowly ossify (turn to bone) after injury; sufferers are gradually encased in a second skeleton.

Proton beam therapy, a precision form of radiation oncology, deposits most of its energy at a Bragg peak inside the tumor rather than passing through surrounding tissue, reducing collateral damage — especially important in pediatric cancers near critical structures.

Stem cell therapy using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), discovered by Shinya Yamanaka in 2006 (2012 Nobel Prize), allows scientists to grow patient-specific tissue for transplant without the ethical concerns of embryonic stem cells.
The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003 after 13 years and $3 billion, sequenced all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA; today a complete genome can be sequenced in about a day for under $1,000.

Liquid biopsies — detecting circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in blood — enable early cancer detection, monitoring of treatment response, and identification of resistance mutations without invasive tissue biopsy.
The electroencephalogram (EEG) was developed by Hans Berger in 1924; it records electrical brain activity through scalp electrodes and remains essential for diagnosing epilepsy and sleep disorders.

Hemophilia A results from deficiency of clotting factor VIII; gene therapy using AAV vectors to deliver functional factor VIII gene has produced multi-year remission from bleeding in clinical trials, approaching a functional cure.

Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) is a fatal disease caused by misfolded transthyretin protein accumulating in organs; patisiran, the first FDA-approved RNAi drug (2018), silences the TTR gene and halts disease progression.
The germ theory of disease was established by Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch in the 1860s–1880s; Koch's postulates (1884) set criteria for proving a specific microorganism causes a specific disease.

Surgical robots such as the da Vinci system (FDA-approved 2000) give surgeons enhanced dexterity via robotic arms; they are used in over 6 million procedures annually, including prostatectomies and cardiac valve repair.

The total artificial heart (TAH), used as a bridge to transplant in end-stage biventricular heart failure, replaces both ventricles with a mechanical pump; SynCardia's TAH has been implanted in over 1,800 patients worldwide.

Acupuncture, originating in China over 2,000 years ago, was included in the WHO's Traditional Medicine Strategy 2019–2025; evidence supports its efficacy for chronic pain, chemotherapy-induced nausea, and post-operative pain.

Spinal cord stimulation (SCS), FDA-approved for chronic pain, delivers mild electrical impulses to the spinal cord via implanted electrodes; newer closed-loop SCS systems adjust stimulation in real time based on neural feedback.

Epidural anesthesia for labor pain, introduced clinically in the 1940s, is now used in over 60% of US deliveries; it works by injecting local anesthetic into the epidural space, blocking nerve signals from the uterus and cervix.

The Turing test for artificial intelligence was proposed in 1950; in medicine, an analogous question is whether AI diagnostics can match or exceed expert clinicians — studies show AI now equals or surpasses dermatologists in melanoma detection.

The opioid crisis in the United States was fueled in part by Purdue Pharma's aggressive marketing of OxyContin starting in 1996, claiming low addiction risk; over 500,000 Americans died of opioid overdoses between 1999 and 2020.

Naloxone (Narcan), an opioid antagonist that reverses overdose within minutes, has saved hundreds of thousands of lives; it is increasingly available over the counter and via nasal spray in many countries.

Fentanyl is approximately 100 times more potent than morphine; illicitly manufactured fentanyl, often mixed into other drugs, has become the primary driver of the fourth wave of the US opioid epidemic.

The endocannabinoid system, discovered in the 1990s while studying THC receptors, is a widespread signaling system modulating pain, appetite, mood, and memory; it provided the rationale for medical cannabis.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression in 2008, uses magnetic fields to stimulate nerve cells in the prefrontal cortex; it is non-invasive and requires no anesthesia.

Ketamine, an anesthetic since the 1960s, was found to produce rapid antidepressant effects within hours; esketamine (Spravato) nasal spray was FDA-approved in 2019 for treatment-resistant depression, the first new mechanism in decades.

The DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, 2013) dropped the 'bereavement exclusion' for depression, sparking debate about pathologizing normal grief — illustrating the tension between medicine and human experience.

Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), refined from its controversial 1938 origins, is now performed under general anesthesia with muscle relaxants; it remains the most rapidly effective treatment for severe depression and acute suicidality.

Psilocybin-assisted therapy received FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation in 2018 for treatment-resistant depression; clinical trials show remission rates of over 30% after just one or two sessions, far outperforming standard antidepressants.

Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare genetic disorder causing insatiable hunger, intellectual disability, and behavioral problems; it results from loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15 and affects 1 in 15,000 people.

Angelman syndrome, caused by loss of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene on chromosome 15, causes severe intellectual disability, seizures, and characteristic 'happy demeanor'; it affects 1 in 12,000 people and has no approved cure.

Rett syndrome, caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome, causes progressive neurological deterioration in girls after apparently normal early development; trofinetide (Daybue), the first FDA-approved treatment, was approved in 2023.

Tetanus toxoid, developed by Gaston Ramon at the Pasteur Institute in 1924, is one of the safest and most effective vaccines; it works by immunizing against the bacterial toxin rather than the bacterium itself.

Maternal tetanus immunization protects newborns through transplacental antibody transfer; neonatal tetanus killed an estimated 787,000 babies in 1988 — a number reduced to under 30,000 by 2018 through vaccination campaigns.
Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, has been known since antiquity; multi-drug therapy introduced by WHO in 1982 has cured over 16 million people, and transmission is now rare in most countries.

Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by triatomine bugs in Latin America, affects 8 million people and is a leading cause of heart failure in endemic regions; it is chronically underdiagnosed even in immigrant populations.

Sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis), caused by Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted by tsetse flies, causes neurological deterioration and is fatal without treatment; fexinidazole became the first oral treatment approved in 2018.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), transmitted by sandfly bites, is fatal without treatment and affects the world's poorest populations; a single-dose liposomal amphotericin B treatment has achieved over 95% cure rates in South Asia.
Medical ultrasound was developed in the 1950s when physicians applied SONAR technology to medicine; Ian Donald in Glasgow pioneered obstetric ultrasound in 1958, transforming prenatal care worldwide.

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was introduced in 1960 by Kouwenhoven, Jude, and Knickerbocker; combined with mouth-to-mouth ventilation described by Peter Safar, it formed the basis of modern basic life support.

The automated external defibrillator (AED) was developed in the 1970s; public access AED programs have increased survival from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest to over 50% in some communities when bystanders use them promptly.

The discovery of the Rh blood group system in 1940 by Karl Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener explained hemolytic disease of the newborn; anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis now prevents Rh incompatibility deaths.

Apheresis — separating blood into components and returning some to the donor — allows collection of platelets, plasma, or specific cells; therapeutic plasma exchange can treat rare conditions like thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

Sickle cell disease was the first molecular disease described by Linus Pauling in 1949; it results from a single point mutation (glutamic acid to valine at position 6 of beta-globin) and is the most common severe monogenic disorder worldwide.

Hydroxyurea, the first disease-modifying therapy for sickle cell disease (FDA-approved 1998), reduces painful crises by inducing fetal hemoglobin production; it is inexpensive but still severely underutilized in Africa where the disease burden is highest.

Closed-loop insulin delivery systems (artificial pancreas) use continuous glucose monitors and insulin pumps controlled by algorithms to automatically adjust insulin doses; they dramatically reduce HbA1c and hypoglycemic episodes in type 1 diabetes.

GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) mimic the gut hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 to suppress appetite and lower blood sugar; clinical trials showed 15–20% body weight reductions, transforming obesity treatment.

Bariatric surgery (gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy) produces remission of type 2 diabetes in 60–80% of patients; it works not just through caloric restriction but through gut hormone changes that improve insulin sensitivity independently of weight loss.

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), popularly called angioplasty, uses a balloon-tipped catheter to open blocked coronary arteries; when combined with stenting it has dramatically reduced mortality from heart attacks since the 1980s.

Drug-eluting stents, introduced in the early 2000s, release anti-proliferative drugs (e.g., sirolimus, paclitaxel) to prevent restenosis after angioplasty, reducing repeat intervention rates from 25% to under 5%.

The BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, discovered in 1994–1995 by Mary-Claire King and colleagues, when mutated substantially increase lifetime risks of breast (up to 85%) and ovarian (up to 44%) cancer; their discovery enabled targeted risk-reduction surgeries.

PARP inhibitors such as olaparib exploit synthetic lethality in BRCA-mutated tumors by blocking a DNA repair pathway cancer cells depend on; they were the first precision oncology drugs based on this concept, approved for ovarian cancer in 2014.

Theranostics — combining a diagnostic and therapeutic agent in one — is used in nuclear medicine; lutetium-177 DOTATATE (Lutathera) both images and delivers targeted radiation to neuroendocrine tumors, approved by FDA in 2018.

Imatinib (Gleevec), approved in 2001 for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), was the first successful kinase inhibitor cancer drug; it turned a once-fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition and triggered the precision oncology revolution.

Vaccination with BCG (Bacille Calmette-Guérin) for tuberculosis, introduced in 1921, remains the most widely administered vaccine in history; it is given at birth in over 100 countries and provides strong protection against severe childhood TB.

The WHO declared tuberculosis a global public health emergency in 1993; TB remains the world's deadliest single infectious pathogen, killing 1.3 million people in 2022, more than HIV/AIDS, with drug-resistant TB posing the greatest ongoing challenge.

Bedaquiline, approved in 2012 by the FDA under accelerated approval, was the first new anti-tuberculosis drug in 40 years; it targets the mycobacterial ATP synthase, a completely novel mechanism not shared with human cells.
Dialysis, developed by Willem Kolff in the Netherlands during World War II using sausage casings and orange juice cans, now sustains over 3.5 million people with kidney failure worldwide.

Peritoneal dialysis uses the lining of the patient's abdominal cavity as a filter; it can be performed at home overnight via automated cyclers, offering flexibility unavailable with center-based hemodialysis.

The first successful pancreas transplant was performed at the University of Minnesota in 1966; pancreas transplantation can restore normal glucose regulation and eliminate insulin dependence in type 1 diabetics.

Heart valve repair and replacement have transformed from high-risk open-heart surgery to catheter-based procedures; TAVR (transcatheter aortic valve replacement), introduced in 2002 by Alain Cribier, is now performed in patients too frail for surgery.

The Heimlich maneuver, described by Henry Heimlich in 1974, uses abdominal thrusts to expel foreign-body airway obstruction; it has saved thousands of lives from choking and became a standard first aid technique worldwide.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) affects motor neurons and is almost universally fatal within 3–5 years; Stephen Hawking's survival for 55 years was exceptional, and tofersen (Qalsody), the first ASO therapy for a genetic form, was approved in 2023.

The ALS Ice Bucket Challenge in 2014 raised over $220 million globally and directly funded the discovery of the NEK1 gene, one of the most common ALS genetic risk factors, illustrating the impact of social media on research funding.

Huntington's disease is caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene; the number of repeats predicts age of onset with remarkable precision — a finding that makes presymptomatic genetic testing possible but raises profound ethical questions.

Tay-Sachs disease, caused by deficiency of hexosaminidase A, accumulates GM2 ganglioside in neurons and is fatal in infancy; carrier screening programs among Ashkenazi Jewish communities have reduced incidence by over 90%.

Niemann-Pick disease type C causes cholesterol trapping inside cells; miglustat (Zavesca), originally developed for Gaucher disease, received orphan designation for NPC and slows neurological deterioration.

Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS I / Hurler syndrome) causes accumulation of glycosaminoglycans causing progressive multiorgan damage; enzyme replacement with laronidase and hematopoietic stem cell transplant in early infancy can significantly alter the disease course.

The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Undiagnosed Diseases Program, launched in 2008, uses cutting-edge genomics to diagnose patients who have gone undiagnosed for years; it has solved about 25% of the cases it accepts, often identifying novel diseases.
The EUROPLAN and NORD networks have established that there are over 7,000 recognized rare diseases, yet only about 5% have an approved treatment; collectively they affect 300 million people globally.

Real-world evidence (RWE) gathered from electronic health records, insurance claims, and patient registries is increasingly used by regulators to supplement clinical trial data, particularly for rare diseases where large trials are impossible.
The microbiome of the human gut contains approximately 38 trillion bacteria — roughly equal to the number of human cells — and collectively encodes 150 times more genes than the human genome.

Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) involves transferring stool from a healthy donor to a patient; it cures recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection in over 90% of cases and is now FDA-approved via the products Rebyota and Vowst.

The vaginal microbiome dominated by Lactobacillus species is associated with protection against preterm birth and sexually transmitted infections; dysbiosis (bacterial vaginosis) affects 30% of reproductive-age women and is linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Neonatal meningitis most commonly caused by Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is prevented by intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis in colonized mothers; universal prenatal GBS screening has reduced early-onset disease by 80% in developed countries.

Photodynamic therapy (PDT) uses photosensitizing agents that accumulate in abnormal tissue and, when activated by light, generate reactive oxygen species that destroy tumors; it is used for esophageal cancer, Barrett's esophagus, and certain skin cancers.

Transoral robotic surgery (TORS) uses the da Vinci robot to remove oropharyngeal cancers through the mouth, avoiding disfiguring incisions in the neck; it has transformed treatment of HPV-positive throat cancers.

Diagnostic error is estimated to affect 12 million Americans annually, with serious harm in 40,000–80,000 cases; the most commonly missed diagnoses are vascular events, infections, and cancers collectively termed the 'Big Three.'

Telemedicine use increased 38-fold in the United States in the first three months of COVID-19 (2020); it has proven particularly effective for mental health, chronic disease management, and dermatology consultations.

Syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum, has four stages; congenital syphilis is re-emerging globally, with the CDC reporting a 32% increase in US cases in 2022 — the highest rate since 1991 — partly attributable to reduced screening during the pandemic.

HPV (human papillomavirus) vaccination with Gardasil 9 prevents infection against nine strains responsible for 90% of cervical cancers and most anal, oropharyngeal, penile, vaginal, and vulvar cancers; widespread vaccination could eliminate cervical cancer.

Hepatitis C, caused by HCV, was identified only in 1989 by Michael Houghton; by 2020, direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) could cure over 95% of infections in 8–12 weeks, transforming a once-fatal liver disease into a curable infection — earning Houghton the 2020 Nobel Prize.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with tenofovir/emtricitabine (Truvada) reduces HIV acquisition risk by over 99% when taken daily; long-acting injectable cabotegravir given every two months has since proven even more effective.

The Ryan White CARE Act (1990) was the largest federally funded program for HIV/AIDS in the US; it improved outcomes by funding care for uninsured and underinsured patients and became a model for HIV treatment programs worldwide.

Ventricular assist devices (VADs) mechanically support failing hearts by supplementing or replacing ventricular pumping; the HeartMate 3 continuous-flow LVAD has a 2-year survival rate exceeding 80% in end-stage heart failure patients awaiting transplant.

Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects 1% of all births and is the most common birth defect; advances in pediatric cardiac surgery have transformed survival — over 90% of children born with CHD now reach adulthood in high-income countries.

Neonatal intensive care has reduced mortality of extremely preterm infants (<28 weeks gestation) from near 100% in the 1960s to under 20% today through surfactant therapy, advanced ventilation, and antenatal corticosteroids.

Surfactant replacement therapy for premature infants with respiratory distress syndrome, developed in the 1980s by Tetsuro Fujiwara, reduced mortality in premature babies by approximately 40% and is now standard worldwide.

Ex-vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) keeps donor lungs breathing outside the body at body temperature to recondition and assess their quality, significantly expanding the pool of usable donor lungs for transplantation.

Machine perfusion of donor kidneys at body temperature before transplantation reduces delayed graft function compared to cold storage; it was FDA-approved in 2021 and could substantially increase the number of successful transplants performed.

The CONSORT statement (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials), first published in 1996 and updated in 2010, established transparency standards for RCT reporting, substantially improving the quality and reproducibility of clinical research.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses pooling data from multiple RCTs provide the highest level of evidence in medicine; the Cochrane Collaboration, founded in 1993, maintains over 10,000 reviews that guide clinical practice worldwide.

The replication crisis in biomedicine — where many landmark studies cannot be reproduced — was highlighted by the Reproducibility Project (2015), which found only about 50% of published cancer biology findings replicated.

Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variants affect drug response; the FDA now includes pharmacogenomic information in labels for over 300 drugs — for example, CYP2D6 variants determine codeine metabolism, with poor metabolizers at risk of toxicity.

The Expanded Access (compassionate use) pathway allows patients with serious conditions to access investigational drugs outside clinical trials; it has saved lives but raises equity concerns when access depends on patient resources and advocacy.

The thalidomide tragedy (1957–1962) — a morning sickness drug causing 10,000 babies to be born with limb malformations — directly led to the Kefauver-Harris Amendment (1962), requiring proof of safety and efficacy before FDA drug approval.

Ivermectin, developed by William Campbell and Satoshi Omura (2015 Nobel Prize), revolutionized treatment of onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis; Merck has donated over 4 billion doses since 1987 through the Mectizan Donation Program.

The concept of 'One Health' was formally articulated in the 2004 Manhattan Principles, which recognized that human, animal, and environmental health are inseparably linked and that multisectoral collaboration is essential to address emerging infectious diseases.

Avian influenza H5N1 has circulated in birds since 1997; its case fatality rate in human infections is approximately 60%, the highest for any influenza strain — a pandemic caused by an H5N1 variant adapted for human transmission is a WHO priority concern.

Monkeypox (mpox), declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern by WHO in 2022 during its global outbreak, is caused by an Orthopoxvirus related to smallpox; cross-protective immunity from smallpox vaccination has declined as vaccination ended in the 1970s.

Nanobodies — single-domain antibody fragments derived from camelid antibodies — are smaller and more stable than conventional antibodies, can penetrate dense tumors more effectively, and are advancing as diagnostics and therapeutics.

PROTAC (proteolysis-targeting chimera) molecules recruit the cell's own protein degradation machinery (ubiquitin-proteasome system) to destroy disease-causing proteins entirely — an approach that can target previously 'undruggable' proteins.

Organoids — miniature lab-grown organs derived from stem cells — can recapitulate the structure and function of intestines, kidneys, brains, and other organs, enabling personalized drug testing and disease modeling.

Brain organoids (cerebral organoids) grown from iPSCs can recapitulate early human brain development; they have been used to study microcephaly caused by the Zika virus — finding a pathological mechanism within weeks of the outbreak.

The epigenome — chemical modifications to DNA and histones that regulate gene expression without altering the genetic code — can be reprogrammed by environment, stress, and diet; epigenetic drugs have been approved for cancers including MDS and lymphoma.

Telomeres — protective caps on chromosomes — shorten with each cell division; telomerase maintains them in stem cells and cancer cells; Elizabeth Blackburn, Carol Greider, and Jack Szostak won the 2009 Nobel Prize for this discovery.

Exosomes — nano-sized vesicles released by cells containing proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids — serve as intercellular messengers and are being harnessed as drug delivery vehicles and as cancer biomarkers in liquid biopsies.

The complement system — a cascade of proteins in innate immunity — can be pathologically over-activated; eculizumab, first approved in 2007 for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, was one of the most expensive drugs in the world and transformed a fatal disease.

The blood-brain barrier (BBB) — formed by tight junctions in brain capillary endothelial cells — blocks 98% of small molecules and nearly all large-molecule drugs from reaching the brain, posing the central challenge of CNS drug delivery.

Focused ultrasound can temporarily open the blood-brain barrier by causing microbubble oscillations in brain capillaries, enabling drug delivery to brain tumors; it is entering clinical trials for glioblastoma, Parkinson's, and Alzheimer's disease.

Anti-VEGF therapy (e.g., ranibizumab/Lucentis, bevacizumab/Avastin) inhibits vascular endothelial growth factor to halt abnormal blood vessel growth; it transformed outcomes for wet age-related macular degeneration and remains a cornerstone of retinal therapy.

Optical coherence tomography (OCT), developed in the 1990s, uses light wave interference to generate micrometer-resolution cross-sectional images of the retina; it has become the most widely used imaging tool in ophthalmology and is also used in cardiology.

Gene therapy for Leber congenital amaurosis type 10 using adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors successfully restored vision in patients with CEP290 mutations in a 2023 trial — representing a CRISPR in-vivo editing approach directly applied in the human eye.

Glenohumeral osteoarthritis and rotator cuff tears affect millions, but platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections derived from a patient's own blood concentrate growth factors to accelerate healing — though evidence on efficacy remains mixed.

3D bioprinting uses bioinks containing living cells to fabricate tissue constructs layer by layer; researchers have printed functional kidney tubules, cardiac patches, and tracheas, moving toward printable organ transplants.

Decellularized organ scaffolds — where all cells are removed from a donor organ leaving only the extracellular matrix — can be repopulated with a recipient's own cells to create a personalized organ, eliminating rejection risk.

The 'exposome' — the totality of environmental exposures from conception to death — complements the genome as a driver of disease; WHO estimates 23% of global deaths are caused by modifiable environmental factors.

Antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) in hospitals use evidence-based protocols to optimize antibiotic prescribing, reducing inappropriate use and slowing the emergence of antimicrobial resistance; they are recommended by WHO globally.

Alexander Fleming's 1928 discovery that the mold Penicillium notatum lysed bacteria was accidental; penicillin was not purified for clinical use until Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's work in 1940 — all three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is classified by WHO as a 'Priority 1 Critical' pathogen; infections caused by it are nearly untreatable with conventional antibiotics, carrying mortality rates of 40–50% in hospital settings.

The MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) crisis in hospitals has been substantially reduced in many countries through contact precautions and decolonization protocols using mupirocin nasal ointment and chlorhexidine washes.
