Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) provides heart-lung bypass outside the body for patients with otherwise fatal cardiac or respiratory failure; ECMO use expanded dramatically during the COVID-19 pandemic and in 2022 was used in over 20,000 patients per year worldwide; survival to hospital discharge ranges from 40–60% in appropriately selected patients.

Biomarkers in medicine — measurable biological indicators of normal or pathological processes — have transformed diagnosis and monitoring; troponin (cardiac muscle protein) is released into blood within hours of myocardial infarction and high-sensitivity troponin assays now detect heart attacks that would have been missed by older tests.

Blood type compatibility for transfusion was established by Karl Landsteiner's discovery of ABO blood groups (Nobel Prize 1930); the additional Rh system discovery in 1940 completed the most clinically important compatibility system — Rh-negative mothers carrying Rh-positive fetuses require Rh immunoglobulin (Rhogam) to prevent hemolytic disease of the newborn.

Plasma transfusion, particularly convalescent plasma, has been used experimentally in epidemics since the 1918 influenza pandemic; its use in COVID-19 treatment failed to show benefit in large trials, illustrating how historically accepted interventions often fail to withstand rigorous clinical trial scrutiny — a lesson central to evidence-based medicine.

The concept of sepsis has been revised three times: Sepsis-1 (1991) defined it by presence of infection plus SIRS criteria; Sepsis-2 (2001) elaborated severity levels; Sepsis-3 (2016) redefined sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction identified by a SOFA score change of ≥2, dropping SIRS and recognizing that the host response, not infection alone, drives organ damage.

source.name: Journal of the American Medical Association

text: Dialysis access — the surgical creation of an arteriovenous fistula in the forearm, usually by connecting the cephalic vein to the radial artery — is considered the 'lifeline' of hemodialysis patients; the Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) guideline 'Fistula First' has increased the proportion of patients using fistulas from 24% (1997) to over 65% (2020).

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2023 was awarded to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for their work on mRNA modifications enabling vaccines; over the full history of the prize (1901–2023), the most represented topics are infectious disease, physiology and biochemistry of hormones, genetics/molecular biology, and neuroscience.

Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy for obstructive sleep apnea, first described by Colin Sullivan in 1981, prevents airway collapse during sleep; untreated severe sleep apnea increases cardiovascular mortality risk by 2–5 fold, and CPAP therapy improves blood pressure, cognitive function, and quality of life.

Functional MRI (fMRI), which maps brain activity by detecting changes in blood oxygenation (BOLD signal) introduced by Seiji Ogawa in 1990, has transformed neuroscience; fMRI studies of brain network activity during rest ('default mode network') revealed that the brain is highly active even at rest, fundamentally changing understanding of brain organization.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), an MRI technique that traces water diffusion along nerve fiber tracts, allows non-invasive mapping of white matter pathways ('tractography') in the brain; it is used to plan neurosurgical tumor resections to avoid eloquent tracts and to study connectivity abnormalities in autism, schizophrenia, and traumatic brain injury.

PET scanning (positron emission tomography), combining radiotracer imaging with CT, can detect amyloid plaques in living brains — a major advancement in Alzheimer's research; amyloid PET imaging changed the diagnosis of Alzheimer's from a clinical diagnosis (confirmed only at autopsy) to a biological diagnosis achievable during life.

Lecanemab (Leqembi), an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody approved by the FDA in 2023, is the first Alzheimer's drug shown to slow cognitive decline (by approximately 27%) in early Alzheimer's disease; its approval represents a watershed moment after decades of failed trials, though brain microhemorrhage side effects require MRI monitoring.

Tau proteins, which normally stabilize neuronal microtubules, form neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies; tau pathology correlates more closely with cognitive decline than amyloid burden, and tau-targeting therapies are a major focus of current Alzheimer's drug development.

Multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune demyelinating disease, has been transformed from a relentlessly progressive disorder to a manageable chronic condition by disease-modifying therapies; natalizumab (2004) reduced relapses by 68% and the highly effective anti-CD20 therapies (ocrelizumab, 2017) reduce not only relapses but brain atrophy.

The discovery that the brain can generate new neurons in adulthood (adult neurogenesis) in the hippocampus, overturning the dogma that the adult brain is fixed, was made by Fred Gage and colleagues in 1998; adult neurogenesis is regulated by exercise, stress, and antidepressants, linking brain plasticity to mental health interventions.

Epigenetics — heritable changes in gene expression without DNA sequence change — plays a major role in aging; DNA methylation clocks (Horvath clock) estimate biological age from methylation patterns with remarkable accuracy and can predict mortality and disease risk independently of chronological age.

Senolytic drugs, which selectively kill senescent ('zombie') cells that accumulate with aging and drive inflammation, are being tested in clinical trials for osteoarthritis, diabetic kidney disease, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; mouse studies show they extend healthy lifespan, and human trials aim to translate this into human healthspan extension.

The Global Burden of Disease study, led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), is the most comprehensive worldwide observational epidemiological study, quantifying health loss from hundreds of diseases, injuries, and risk factors across all countries; its findings consistently show ischemic heart disease, stroke, and lower respiratory infection as the top global killers.

source.name: Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation

text: Primary health care, defined by the 1978 Alma-Ata Declaration as 'essential health care made universally accessible to individuals and families in the community by means acceptable to them,' has been shown to be the most cost-effective foundation for health systems; countries with strong primary care have better health outcomes at lower cost than those centered on specialist and hospital care.

Universal health coverage (UHC), a WHO goal for all countries, means all people receive the health services they need without suffering financial hardship; approximately 4.5 billion people worldwide currently lack access to essential health services, and health-related financial catastrophe pushes over 100 million into poverty annually.

The social determinants of health — income, education, housing, employment, social inclusion, and access to nutritious food — account for 30–55% of health outcomes by WHO estimates; addressing poverty and inequality is consequently at least as important as any medical intervention for improving population health.

source.name: WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health

text: Community health workers (CHWs), lay members of communities trained to provide basic health education and services, have proven highly effective in low-income settings; Ethiopia's Health Extension Workers program, training over 38,000 women in rural communities since 2004, contributed to dramatic reductions in under-5 mortality and maternal mortality.

Task-shifting — delegating medical tasks from specialist physicians to less specialized health workers — has become essential in low-resource settings; studies in sub-Saharan Africa show nurse-initiated HIV antiretroviral therapy achieves outcomes equivalent to physician-initiated therapy, demonstrating that much of medicine's work can be safely performed by appropriately trained non-physicians.

The first randomized controlled trial in medicine is considered the 1948 MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis, designed by Austin Bradford Hill; it established the placebo-controlled double-blind RCT as the gold standard for evaluating medical interventions and transformed how medicine generates and evaluates evidence.

The p-value crisis in medicine and science — where the arbitrary 0.05 threshold for statistical significance is widely misunderstood and misused — has contributed to a replication crisis; a 2015 Nature survey found that over 70% of researchers failed to reproduce published experiments, prompting calls for pre-registration, open data, and larger sample sizes.

Adaptive clinical trials, which allow pre-specified modifications to study design based on accumulating data, have reduced the time and cost to identify effective COVID-19 treatments; the UK RECOVERY trial (2020) tested multiple therapies simultaneously in a platform design that rapidly identified dexamethasone as effective while ruling out hydroxychloroquine.

Wearable health technology market, valued at over $60 billion, now includes FDA-cleared devices that detect atrial fibrillation (Apple Watch), measure blood glucose non-invasively, track sleep stages, and measure blood oxygen saturation; consumer wearables have detected undiagnosed conditions in millions and are changing the role of patients in their own health monitoring.

The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003 at a cost of $3 billion, sequenced the 3-billion-base-pair human genome; the cost of sequencing a whole human genome has since fallen from $100 million (2001) to under $1,000 (2014) to under $200 (2023), enabling population genomics, newborn sequencing, and routine clinical genomics.

Polygenic risk scores (PRS), which sum the effects of thousands of common genetic variants to estimate disease risk, are emerging as clinical tools for cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and type 2 diabetes; individuals in the top 1% of PRS for coronary artery disease have 3-fold higher lifetime risk than average, comparable to monogenic familial hypercholesterolemia.

Regenerative medicine's holy grail — regrowing functional hearts, kidneys, and livers — may be achievable through decellularization: stripping a donor organ of its cells to leave a protein scaffold, then reseeding it with the patient's own cells; rat hearts have been recellularized and shown spontaneous beating activity.

Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy delivers short strands of RNA-like molecules that bind to and silence specific mRNA targets; nusinersen (Spinraza) for SMA, mipomersen for familial hypercholesterolemia, and inclisiran for LDL reduction exemplify how ASO therapy has moved from concept to approved treatments for previously untreatable genetic conditions.

Digital therapeutics (DTx) — software-based medical interventions that treat diseases with clinical evidence as rigorous as drugs — received FDA authorization with Pear Therapeutics' reSET for substance use disorder (2017); DTx apps for insomnia (Somryst), ADHD (EndeavorRx), and PTSD are being prescribed like medications and covered by some insurers.

Surgical simulation using high-fidelity mannequins and virtual-reality platforms allows trainees to rehearse complex procedures — from laparoscopic cholecystectomy to cardiac catheterization — without risk to patients, and studies show simulation-trained residents make significantly fewer operative errors.

source.name: Journal of the American College of Surgeons

text: The Cochrane Collaboration, founded in 1993, produces systematic reviews that synthesize all available randomized controlled trial evidence on a clinical question; its reviews are considered the gold standard for evidence-based medicine and are freely accessible via the Cochrane Library.

Evidence-based medicine (EBM), a term coined by Gordon Guyatt at McMaster University in 1990, integrates the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values — replacing the prior tradition of deference to senior authority and anecdotal experience.

Telemedicine consultations surged over 3,800% in the United States during the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, and post-pandemic utilization remains dramatically higher than pre-2020 baselines, particularly for mental health and chronic disease management.

Global surgery access is profoundly unequal: the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (2015) estimated that 5 billion people lack access to safe, affordable surgical care, and 143 million additional procedures are needed annually in low- and middle-income countries.

Tropical medicine as a formal specialty emerged in the late 19th century with Patrick Manson's discovery that mosquitoes transmit filariasis (1877) and Ronald Ross's demonstration that Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria parasites (1897), earning Ross the Nobel Prize.

source.name: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine

text: Military medicine has driven major advances in trauma care: tourniquets, once thought dangerous for extended use, were rehabilitated by combat experience in Iraq and Afghanistan and are now standard pre-hospital treatment for limb hemorrhage, credited with saving thousands of lives.

source.name: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

text: Space medicine addresses unique physiological challenges of microgravity including bone density loss (~1–2% per month), muscle atrophy, fluid shifts toward the head, vision impairment (VIIP syndrome), and altered immune function — all intensely studied aboard the ISS.

Forensic medicine (forensic pathology) determines cause and manner of death through autopsy; the specialty was formalized in Scotland in 1807 when Andrew Duncan established the first Chair of Medical Jurisprudence at the University of Edinburgh.

Narrative medicine, developed by Rita Charon at Columbia University in 2000, trains clinicians to read and write literary narratives of illness to improve empathy, attention, and the therapeutic relationship — and is now a graduate program offering a Master of Science degree.

Cardiothoracic surgery encompasses operations on the heart, lungs, and great vessels; the first successful open-heart surgery using cardiopulmonary bypass was performed by John Gibbon on May 6, 1953, at Jefferson Medical College using a heart-lung machine he spent 23 years developing.

Neurosurgery pioneered the use of the operating microscope in 1957 by Theodore Kurze for spinal tumor removal; today microsurgical techniques allow resection of tumors within millimeters of eloquent brain cortex while preserving function.

Orthopedic surgery's most-performed elective procedure is total knee arthroplasty; over 790,000 knee replacements are performed annually in the United States, with implant survivorship exceeding 90% at 15 years due to improvements in prosthetic materials and fixation techniques.

Plastic and reconstructive surgery traces its modern roots to the WWI work of Harold Gillies at the Queen's Hospital, Sidcup, where he developed skin pedicle flap techniques to reconstruct the shattered faces of soldiers — treating over 5,000 cases and publishing Plastic Surgery of the Face in 1920.

source.name: British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons

text: Urological surgery for bladder cancer increasingly uses photodynamic diagnosis (PDD): patients receive a photosensitizing agent (hexaminolevulinate) that causes tumor cells to fluoresce bright pink under blue light, enabling surgeons to detect and resect tumors invisible under white light.

Vascular surgery has been transformed by endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), first performed by Juan Parodi in 1991: a stent-graft is delivered through small groin incisions and deployed inside the aortic aneurysm, avoiding the high-risk open abdominal repair and reducing 30-day mortality from ~5% to ~1.6%.

Ophthalmic surgery's most common procedure — phacoemulsification cataract surgery — uses an ultrasonic probe to emulsify the clouded lens, which is then aspirated and replaced with a foldable intraocular lens through an incision of ~2.2 mm; over 3 million procedures are done annually in the US.

Otolaryngology (ENT) surgery pioneered cochlear implantation: the first FDA-approved cochlear implant for adults came in 1984, and devices now provide meaningful hearing to over 700,000 recipients worldwide, making severe-to-profound sensorineural deafness effectively treatable.

Medical simulation using standardized patients — trained actors who portray patients with scripted symptoms and emotional responses — allows medical students and residents to practice history-taking, physical examination, and difficult conversations in a safe, assessable environment.

The number needed to treat (NNT) is a core evidence-based medicine metric: it represents how many patients must receive a treatment for one to benefit compared to control; statins for primary prevention have an NNT of ~140 over 5 years, while antibiotics for strep throat have an NNT of ~7 to prevent one case of rheumatic fever.

Schistosomiasis, a parasitic disease caused by blood flukes, infects ~250 million people in 78 countries — second only to malaria in global parasitic disease burden; the drug praziquantel, developed in 1972, treats all species and costs less than $0.20 per dose.

Combat casualty care introduced the 'Tactical Combat Casualty Care' (TCCC) guidelines in 1996, developed by Navy SEAL Frank Butler; they shifted care from the hospital to the point of wounding and are credited with reducing preventable combat deaths from ~25% in Vietnam to ~8% in post-2001 conflicts.

The NASA Twin Study tracked astronaut Scott Kelly and his identical twin brother Mark on Earth for one year (2015–2016), revealing that spaceflight causes telomere elongation, gene expression changes, cognitive decline, and gut microbiome shifts — most but not all reversible after return.

Forensic odontology uses dental records to identify human remains and bite-mark evidence; its most celebrated application was the identification of victims in the 1985 Gander, Newfoundland air disaster — and dental records were crucial to identifying victims of the 9/11 attacks.

Medical humanities encompasses history, literature, philosophy, ethics, and arts in medical training; programs at NYU Grossman and Yale School of Medicine require humanities coursework, recognizing that physicians who engage with the humanities demonstrate greater empathy and reduced burnout.

The Halstedian model of surgical training — 'See one, do one, teach one' — dominated for over a century but is being replaced by competency-based training, simulation, and structured assessment as duty-hour restrictions limit trainee operative exposure.

Remote patient monitoring (RPM) using connected devices — glucometers, pulse oximeters, blood pressure cuffs, implantable cardiac monitors — transmits real-time physiological data to clinicians; trials show RPM reduces hospital readmissions for heart failure by up to 38%.

Dengue fever, caused by four distinct serotypes of the dengue virus and transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, infects an estimated 390 million people annually; a second infection with a different serotype carries a risk of severe dengue hemorrhagic fever due to antibody-dependent enhancement.

The Damage Control Surgery (DCS) philosophy, developed in the 1990s for combat and major trauma, deliberately performs only life-saving abbreviated operations initially, packing wounds and closing temporarily, then completing definitive repair 24–72 hours later after physiologic resuscitation in the ICU.

source.name: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

text: Astronaut vision impairment — termed Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) — occurs in ~70% of long-duration ISS crew members and involves optic disc edema, globe flattening, and refractive shifts toward hyperopia, potentially caused by chronic cephalad fluid shifts in microgravity.

Forensic toxicology determines whether drugs or poisons contributed to death or impairment; postmortem redistribution — the movement of drugs from tissues into blood after death — can dramatically alter measured concentrations and complicate interpretation, requiring careful sampling from peripheral veins.

The 'illness narrative' concept, articulated by Arthur Kleinman in The Illness Narratives (1988), distinguishes 'disease' (the biomedical pathology) from 'illness' (the patient's lived experience), arguing that physicians must elicit and honor both to deliver effective care.

Minimally invasive cardiac surgery (MICS) uses small right thoracotomy incisions, endoscopic cameras, and port access to repair mitral valves, close atrial septal defects, and perform bypass — reducing blood loss, pain, ICU stay, and time to return to work compared with sternotomy.

GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation), introduced in 2004, provides a systematic framework for rating the quality of evidence and strength of clinical recommendations and is now used by over 100 organizations including WHO, CDC, and most major medical societies.

Task-shifting in global health — training community health workers, nurses, and non-physician clinicians to perform roles traditionally reserved for doctors — has dramatically extended surgical access in sub-Saharan Africa; Mozambique's técnicos de cirurgia perform cesarean sections and emergency laparotomies with outcomes comparable to physicians.

Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), caused by Leishmania donovani and transmitted by sandflies, kills 20,000–30,000 people annually and is fatal if untreated; liposomal amphotericin B achieves >95% cure rates with a single-dose regimen in South Asia, dramatically simplifying treatment.

REBOA (Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta), introduced to trauma surgery in the 2010s from military medicine, uses a balloon catheter inserted through the femoral artery to occlude the aorta and temporize life-threatening torso hemorrhage — a minimally invasive alternative to emergency thoracotomy.

source.name: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

text: Radiation therapy in space is a critical concern: beyond Earth's magnetosphere, astronauts are exposed to galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events that can deliver doses sufficient to exceed NASA's career radiation limits on a single Mars transit, and current shielding materials offer limited protection against high-energy particles.

Forensic entomology uses insect succession patterns on decomposing remains to estimate the postmortem interval (PMI); blow flies (Calliphoridae) typically arrive within minutes of death and their larval development stage can pinpoint time of death to within hours under controlled conditions.

The use of arts in clinical settings — known as arts in health — is evidence-supported: a systematic review in The Lancet found that engaging with visual arts, music, dance, and writing reduces anxiety, pain perception, and hospital length of stay, and enhances immune function.

Pediatric surgery as a specialty was established largely through the work of C. Everett Koop at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia in the 1950s–1970s; he pioneered repair of esophageal atresia, conjoined twin separation, and sacrococcygeal teratoma resection before becoming US Surgeon General.

Publication bias — the tendency for journals to publish positive results over negative or null findings — significantly distorts the evidence base; the Cochrane Collaboration's funnel plot asymmetry tests and prospective trial registration at ClinicalTrials.gov are key tools for detecting and mitigating this bias.

Teledermatology, one of telemedicine's most established store-and-forward applications, allows primary care physicians to photograph skin lesions and receive specialist review within 24–48 hours, reducing wait times from months to days and achieving diagnostic concordance with in-person consultation of over 80%.

Buruli ulcer, caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans and ranking third globally among mycobacterial diseases, destroys skin and soft tissue through a toxin called mycolactone; in 2023, WHO endorsed an 8-week oral rifampicin–clarithromycin regimen that replaces the prior IV-dependent treatment and can be delivered in communities.

Freeze-dried plasma (lyophilized plasma), first used in WWII, has been reintroduced to military medicine as an ideal pre-hospital hemostatic resuscitation fluid; it reconstitutes in minutes, is shelf-stable at room temperature for years, and was adopted by French military in 1994 and increasingly by NATO forces.

Bone loss in astronauts on 6-month ISS missions averages 1–2% per month in weight-bearing bones of the hip and spine; countermeasures include the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED), bisphosphonate pharmacotherapy, and optimized nutrition protocols, but complete recovery after return can take 2–3 years.

Forensic genetics uses short tandem repeat (STR) profiling to establish identity with greater than 1-in-a-quintillion certainty; the FBI's CODIS database contains over 21 million DNA profiles, and cold cases decades old are routinely solved using degraded samples from archived evidence.

Susan Sontag's Illness as Metaphor (1978) argued that diseases like cancer and tuberculosis are laden with harmful cultural metaphors that stigmatize patients and distort medical discourse, becoming a foundational text in medical humanities for critiquing how language shapes the experience of illness.

Laparoscopic (keyhole) surgery, popularized in the late 1980s with Philippe Mouret's first laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Lyon in 1987, has transformed surgery: today over 90% of elective cholecystectomies in high-income countries are performed laparoscopically, with dramatically shorter recovery compared to open surgery.

The Cochrane Review on vitamin C for the common cold (Hemilä, 2013) — one of the most accessed in the library — found that while routine supplementation does not prevent colds in the general population, it halves cold duration in athletes and individuals under extreme physical stress.

Project ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes), launched by Sanjeev Arora at the University of New Mexico in 2003, uses telemedicine video hubs to train rural primary care providers in specialty care — from hepatitis C to chronic pain — bringing specialist knowledge to underserved areas without relocating physicians.

Onchocerciasis (river blindness), caused by the filarial worm Onchocerca volvulus transmitted by Simulium blackflies, is the world's second leading infectious cause of blindness; annual ivermectin distribution has reduced transmission in 11 African countries, and combined ivermectin-doxycycline regimens aim for parasite elimination.

The ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support) course, developed by orthopedic surgeon James Styner after a 1976 light-plane crash killed his wife and critically injured his children with inadequate rural trauma care available, has trained over 1 million physicians in 86 countries in systematic trauma assessment.

Space pharmacology must account for altered drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination in microgravity; studies on ISS crew show reduced gastric motility, altered fluid distribution, and changes in liver enzyme activity — meaning standard Earth doses may not achieve therapeutic levels in orbit.

Bloodstain pattern analysis (BPA), a forensic discipline, reconstructs the dynamics of violent events using the size, shape, distribution, and directionality of blood drops; the angle of impact of an elliptical bloodstain is calculated from the width-to-length ratio using the arcsine function.

source.name: International Association of Bloodstain Pattern Analysts

text: The 'patient as teacher' model in medical education formally incorporates people with lived experience of illness into curricula: programs at Imperial College London and Stanford have patients co-design and deliver sessions on chronic disease, disability, and end-of-life care, measurably improving student empathy scores.

Endoscopic skull-base surgery, pioneered by Heinz Stammberger and further developed in the 1990s, uses the nasal passages as a natural corridor to access tumors of the pituitary gland, olfactory groove, and clivus — avoiding open craniotomy and dramatically reducing recovery time and morbidity.

The 'five-second rule' of evidence-based medicine teaching — that information halves in relevance every five years — is a heuristic driving continuous medical education (CME) requirements; US physicians must complete 50 CME hours annually, and sub-specialty recertification now increasingly emphasizes assessed learning rather than passive attendance.

Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by triatomine 'kissing bugs,' affects ~6–7 million people in Latin America and causes cardiomyopathy and megacolon decades after initial infection; immigration has made it an emerging public health issue in the United States, Spain, and other non-endemic countries.

Hypothermia protocols in trauma and cardiac arrest use therapeutic cooling to reduce metabolic demand and neurological injury; the military has trialled ice-cold saline field resuscitation for penetrating trauma, while hospital targeted temperature management (TTM) at 33–36°C improves neurological outcomes after cardiac arrest.

The International Space Station serves as a unique microgravity laboratory for human physiology research; experiments aboard ISS have advanced understanding of muscle atrophy mechanisms, fluid shifts in the cardiovascular system, and the role of gravity in gene regulation — with direct applications to aging and rehabilitation on Earth.

Digital autopsy (virtual autopsy or 'virtopsy'), pioneered by Michael Thali in Switzerland using CT and MRI scanning of the deceased, can reveal cause of death in many cases non-invasively; it is especially valuable in cases involving religious objections to dissection and in mass-casualty identification.

The graphic medicine movement uses comics and graphic novels to explore illness and medical experience; works like Marisa Acocella Marchetto's Cancer Vixen, David B.'s Epileptic, and Brian Fies's Mom's Cancer are now taught in medical schools as tools for understanding patient perspectives.

Sentinel lymph node biopsy, introduced by Donald Morton in 1990 for melanoma and extended to breast cancer by Armando Giuliano, allows pathological staging of regional lymph nodes by injecting dye or radiotracer that maps the first ('sentinel') draining node — sparing most patients the morbidity of full axillary dissection.

The concept of 'spin' in medical research — the presentation of non-significant results as positive through language choices — is pervasive: a Cochrane analysis found spin in 57% of randomized trial abstracts with non-significant primary outcomes, potentially misleading clinicians and patients.

Telestroke networks allow neurologists at academic hubs to perform real-time video assessment of stroke patients at remote hospitals and guide thrombolysis decisions; studies show tPA administration rates and door-to-needle times at spoke hospitals match those at primary stroke centers when supported by telestroke.

Yaws, a chronic skin disease caused by Treponema pallidum pertenue and affecting children in tropical humid regions, can be cured with a single dose of oral azithromycin; WHO's Morges Strategy aims for eradication by 2030 using mass drug administration — it would be the first disease eradicated using oral antibiotic alone.

The US Military's Joint Trauma System maintains the Department of Defense Trauma Registry — the world's most detailed real-time combat casualty database — which continuously analyzes injury patterns and outcomes to update clinical practice guidelines, creating an unprecedented evidence-based loop between battlefield and policy.

source.name: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

text: Telemedicine for mental health (telepsychiatry) has been shown in multiple randomized trials to be non-inferior to in-person psychiatric consultation for diagnostic accuracy, patient satisfaction, and treatment outcomes for depression, PTSD, and schizophrenia — expanding access to rural and incarcerated populations.

Robotic surgery (da Vinci system, FDA approved 2000) is now used in over 1.8 million procedures annually worldwide; the system provides 3D magnification, tremor filtration, and 7-degree-of-freedom instrument articulation — particularly advantageous in confined spaces like the pelvis for radical prostatectomy.

Physician empathy, measurable using validated scales such as the Jefferson Scale of Empathy, declines significantly during medical school and residency — a phenomenon well-documented since the 1950s; narrative medicine, arts curricula, and structured reflection programs are evidence-supported interventions to reverse this erosion.

Transplant surgery's longest-surviving recipient as of 2024 is John McCafferty, who received a heart transplant in 1982 at Harefield Hospital in England and lived for over 30 years with his donor heart — far exceeding expectations and demonstrating the potential durability of cardiac allografts.

The CONSORT statement (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials), first published in 1996 and updated in 2010, provides a checklist of 25 items for reporting randomized controlled trials and is now required by over 600 journals; studies show CONSORT-compliant reports have significantly less reporting bias and higher methodological quality.

Essential Surgery, listed among WHO's essential health services since 2015, includes procedures for obstetric emergencies, injuries, infections, and digestive diseases that are life-saving, time-sensitive, and cost-effective; strengthening surgical systems is now recognized as fundamental to universal health coverage.

Lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis), caused by Wuchereria bancrofti transmitted by mosquitoes, disfigures ~36 million people; the global elimination program uses mass drug administration with ivermectin or diethylcarbamazine plus albendazole, and has reduced transmission in 16 of 72 endemic countries to near-elimination thresholds.

Aeromedical evacuation (MEDEVAC) was revolutionized during the Korean War when helicopters first transported wounded soldiers directly from the battlefield to surgical hospitals, reducing the time to definitive care from hours to minutes and dropping the case fatality rate for wounded American soldiers from 4.5% (WWII) to 2.5%.

Space sickness (Space Adaptation Syndrome) affects ~70% of astronauts during the first 1–3 days in microgravity due to sensory conflict between visual input and vestibular signals; it resolves spontaneously as the brain recalibrates, but poses critical risks if it incapacitates crew during emergency operations.

Forensic anthropology examines skeletal remains to establish biological profile (age, sex, stature, ancestry) and trauma patterns; the discipline gained international prominence in mass grave investigations of genocide victims in Bosnia, Rwanda, and Guatemala, providing evidence for war crimes tribunals.

Paul Farmer's Partners in Health, co-founded in 1987, pioneered the concept of 'accompaniment' in global medicine — embedding healthcare within communities through community health workers, addressing social determinants, and providing direct financial support — demonstrating that high-quality TB and HIV care is achievable even in Haiti.

The ACGME (Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education) 2003 duty-hour reform limiting US residents to 80-hour workweeks sparked debate about whether reduced hours improve trainee wellbeing and patient safety or compromise surgical competency — and Cochrane reviews of the evidence show mixed results.

Ophthalmological telemedicine has transformed diabetic retinopathy screening: automated AI-assisted retinal photography programs in the UK NHS and US VA system detect referable retinopathy without an ophthalmologist present, enabling population-scale screening in primary care clinics.

Trachoma, the world's leading infectious cause of blindness, is caused by repeated Chlamydia trachomatis eye infections transmitted by flies and contact; WHO's SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement) has eliminated trachoma as a public health problem in 17 countries since 1998.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) treats decompression sickness in military divers and air embolism by delivering 100% oxygen at 2–3 atmospheres absolute pressure, dissolving inert gas bubbles and accelerating wound healing; military dive medicine units operate recompression chambers worldwide.

Pharmaceutical countermeasures for space radiation include investigational antioxidants such as amifostine, amino acid supplements, and selective radioprotectors; however, no proven drug currently eliminates the cancer risk from deep-space galactic cosmic ray exposure, making mission architecture (shorter transit times, shielding) the primary mitigation strategy.

The 'CSI effect' — the distortion of juror expectations about forensic evidence due to dramatic TV portrayals — is a documented problem in criminal trials; research shows jurors in cases without DNA evidence are less likely to convict, even when other evidence is compelling, placing unrealistic demands on real forensic science.

source.name: Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology

text: William Osler, widely regarded as the father of modern medical education, introduced bedside teaching at Johns Hopkins in 1889 and authored The Principles and Practice of Medicine — but also wrote extensively on the history of medicine and the humanities, arguing that science alone cannot make a physician.

Fistula surgery for obstetric fistula — a devastating childbirth injury leaving women incontinent and socially ostracized — has been performed at the Addis Ababa Fistula Hospital (founded by Catherine Hamlin in 1974) on over 60,000 Ethiopian women with cure rates exceeding 90%, representing one of the most impactful global surgery programs.

Medical podcasts and point-of-care apps have transformed EBM uptake: UpToDate, used by over 1 million clinicians in 190 countries, provides real-time synthesized clinical recommendations; its use has been independently associated with lower hospital mortality and shorter length of stay in multiple studies.

source.name: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association

text: Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) uses real-time electrophysiological signals — somatosensory evoked potentials, motor evoked potentials, electromyography — during spine and brain surgery to detect impending neural injury before it becomes permanent, reducing post-operative neurological deficits.

The Masimo pulse oximeter, invented by Joe Kiani and Mohamed Diab in the 1990s, solved the longstanding problem of motion artifact in pulse oximetry; it is now standard in anesthesia, ICUs, and was a key tool in detecting silent hypoxia in COVID-19 patients.

The Meakins-Christie Laboratories at McGill University pioneered evidence-based medicine research in respiratory diseases; David Sackett, working there with Gordon Guyatt, co-authored the landmark 1992 JAMA 'Users' Guides to the Medical Literature' series that taught a generation of physicians to critically appraise research.

The Surgeons OverSeas (SOS) Assessment of Surgical Need survey tool quantifies surgical burden in low-income countries by asking households about untreated surgical conditions and unmet need; surveys in Sierra Leone found that 25% of all deaths and 32% of all disability-adjusted life years were attributable to unmet surgical disease.

Sleeping sickness (Human African Trypanosomiasis) caused by Trypanosoma brucei crosses the blood-brain barrier in stage 2, causing the progressive neuropsychiatric symptoms and disrupted sleep-wake cycles that give the disease its name; fexinidazole, an oral drug approved in 2019, replaced the arsenical melarsoprol and dramatically improved treatment safety.

The field of combat medicine spawned the hemostatic dressing revolution: QuikClot Combat Gauze impregnated with kaolin (a clay mineral that activates Factor XII) became the US military's primary hemorrhage control dressing in 2008, and is credited with preventing exsanguination from extremity and junctional wounds.

Telemedicine is closing the stroke treatment gap in stroke deserts: a study of 21 hospitals in 9 US states found that after telestroke implementation, rural hospital tPA usage increased 8-fold, door-to-needle time fell by 25 minutes, and patient outcomes matched those at comprehensive stroke centers.

Hydatid disease (cystic echinococcosis), caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus acquired from dogs and livestock, produces liver cysts that can grow for years undetected; PAIR (Percutaneous Aspiration, Injection, Reaspiration) has largely replaced surgery for uncomplicated hepatic cysts.

MEDEVAC to definitive care has been measured by the 'golden hour' concept — the critical window for trauma treatment popularized by R Adams Cowley at the University of Maryland Shock Trauma Center — though evidence suggests the window is not fixed at one hour; transport time to surgical care remains a crucial determinant of survival.

source.name: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

text: 'Reflection in practice,' a concept developed by philosopher Donald Schön, underpins reflective portfolios required in medical training worldwide; regular written reflection on clinical encounters has been shown in studies to improve clinical reasoning, professionalism, and self-directed learning.

The Safe Surgery Saves Lives campaign by WHO produced the Surgical Safety Checklist in 2008: a 19-item tool completed before anesthesia, before incision, and before leaving the OR; a landmark New England Journal of Medicine study by Atul Gawande showed it reduced major complications by 36% and death by 47% in 8 hospitals across 8 countries.

Cochrane Reviews cover over 8,500 clinical topics; the review on corticosteroids for sore throat found that a single dose of dexamethasone reduces throat pain at 24 hours with an NNT of 5 — a finding that has changed prescribing practice in emergency departments worldwide.

Trauma-informed care (TIC), recognized by SAMHSA as a key framework for healthcare systems, requires providers to understand, recognize, and respond to the effects of all types of trauma — domestic violence, childhood abuse, mass casualty — and to avoid re-traumatization through empathic, patient-centered practice.

Organ Procurement Organizations (OPOs) in the United States coordinate between families of brain-dead or circulatory-dead donors and transplant centers; donation after circulatory death (DCD) protocols have expanded the donor pool by recovering livers, kidneys, and lungs from donors who do not meet brain-death criteria.

The PRISMA statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses), published in 2009 and updated in 2020, provides a 27-item checklist and flow diagram for transparent reporting of systematic reviews; it is endorsed by over 200 journals and cited over 50,000 times.

Acute mountain sickness (AMS) affects up to 75% of trekkers ascending rapidly to altitudes above 2,500 m; acetazolamide (Diamox) prevents AMS by stimulating respiratory compensation for altitude-induced hypoxia, and is an established pharmacoprophylaxis used by climbers and military personnel in high-altitude operations.

Microsurgery for lymphedema using lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA) — connecting microscopic lymphatic channels to tiny veins under a supermicroscope — offers treatment for secondary lymphedema after cancer surgery; surgeons perform anastomoses on vessels as small as 0.3 mm in diameter using 11-0 sutures under 30x magnification.

Telecritical care (tele-ICU) deploys intensivists at central hubs who monitor multiple geographically distant ICUs via two-way audio-video and continuous physiological data streams; multiple studies demonstrate reduction in ICU mortality and length of stay at sites with limited on-site specialist availability.

Scabies, a skin infestation by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, disproportionately affects impoverished communities and can trigger post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatic heart disease through secondary bacterial infection; oral ivermectin mass drug administration campaigns have dramatically reduced community scabies prevalence in island settings.

The Committee on Tactical Combat Casualty Care (CoTCCC), convened since 2002, reviews combat casualty data and updates TCCC guidelines continuously; one landmark change was adoption of tranexamic acid (TXA) in 2011 after the CRASH-2 trial showed it reduced trauma mortality by 1.5 percentage points — saving lives if given within 3 hours.

Behavioral health in space — psychological wellbeing of crews on long-duration missions — is considered among NASA's most significant risks for Mars exploration; isolation, confinement, monotony, communication delays of up to 24 minutes each way, and interpersonal conflict are documented stressors requiring evidence-based countermeasures.

Decomposition stages — fresh, bloat, active decay, advanced decay, skeletonization — depend on temperature, humidity, insect access, and burial conditions; forensic investigators use accumulated degree days (ADD) to standardize time-since-death estimates across variable environmental conditions.

The bioethics movement in medicine traces to the Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972) and the foundational Belmont Report (1979) which articulated three principles — respect for persons (autonomy), beneficence, and justice — that underpin modern research ethics and informed consent requirements worldwide.

source.name: HHS Office for Human Research Protections

text: Hepatobiliary surgery encompassing liver resection (hepatectomy) was once prohibitively dangerous due to hemorrhage; the Pringle maneuver (manual compression of the hepatoduodenal ligament to occlude portal inflow, described in 1908) combined with modern anatomical segmental resection and intraoperative ultrasound has reduced major hepatectomy mortality to below 2% at specialist centers.

Random-effects meta-analysis, a cornerstone method in Cochrane Reviews, pools effect estimates from heterogeneous studies by treating true effect sizes as drawn from a distribution rather than a single value; the DerSimonian-Laird method, introduced in 1986, remains widely used despite ongoing debate about its statistical properties.

Asynchronous ('store-and-forward') telemedicine allows dermatologists, radiologists, and pathologists to review images and reports offline within agreed turnaround times, contrasting with synchronous video visits; the combination of both modalities — a 'hybrid' model — is increasingly used in ophthalmology, dermatology, and wound care.

Soil-transmitted helminths (roundworm, hookworm, whipworm) infect approximately 1.5 billion people globally, impairing child cognitive development and school performance through anemia and malnutrition; WHO's strategy of preventive chemotherapy uses albendazole and mebendazole delivered through school-based mass drug administration programs.

Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) medicine is a military specialty preparing forces and civilian first responders for weapons of mass destruction; the nerve agent antidote atropine auto-injector (EpiPen-style) is carried by US soldiers in theaters where chemical warfare is possible.

Circadian rhythm disruption in space is profound: without natural sunrise-sunset cues, ISS crew experience 16 sunrises per day at orbital speed; NASA uses programmable LED lighting systems tuned to specific wavelengths to suppress or promote melatonin secretion, supporting sleep quality and circadian alignment.

Forensic facial reconstruction — sculpting a face over an unidentified skull using soft-tissue depth markers derived from population databases — is used to generate a recognizable image for public appeals; while not a means of definitive identification, it has led to identifications in numerous cold cases.

Poetry has an established place in medical education: the journal Literature and Medicine and the NYU School of Medicine's 'Bellevue Literary Review' publish work by patients and physicians; programs that incorporate poetry writing in clinical training report improvements in attention to detail, tolerance of ambiguity, and empathic listening.

Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) for pancreatic head cancer involves removing the pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder, common bile duct, and sometimes a portion of the stomach — one of the most technically demanding abdominal operations; 30-day mortality at high-volume centers is below 3%, compared to 15–20% at low-volume hospitals.

The All Trials campaign, launched in 2013 by Ben Goldacre and others, advocates for registration and full reporting of all clinical trials; estimates suggest half of all completed trials are never published, systematically skewing the evidence base and enabling biased prescribing decisions that harm patients.

Low-cost ultrasound in resource-limited settings — the 'FAST' (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) exam — has been adopted in global surgery programs in sub-Saharan Africa and Asia; trained non-physicians using handheld ultrasound devices can detect pneumothorax, hemopericardium, and intraabdominal blood in minutes.

Melioidosis, caused by the environmental bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei endemic in tropical Asia-Pacific soils, infects ~165,000 people annually with ~89,000 deaths — more than leptospirosis or dengue — yet remains 'neglected' in global health funding; it is also classified as a potential bioterrorism agent (Category B).

Operational medicine in extreme environments — including arctic, jungle, and desert warfare — requires tailored protocols; frostbite management was revolutionized by the Wilderness Medical Society's 2014 guidelines recommending field rewarming with warm water immersion and ibuprofen, replacing historic interventions that worsened tissue damage.

Muscle atrophy in space begins within 24–48 hours of weightlessness exposure; both slow-twitch (type I) and fast-twitch (type II) fibers atrophy, with type I fibers converting toward faster phenotypes — changes mirroring those in bedrest and aging, making spaceflight a validated model for studying sarcopenia therapeutics.

Toxicogenomics in forensic medicine uses gene expression patterns in tissues — mRNA signatures of specific genes — as post-mortem biomarkers for cause of death; RNA expression profiles in cardiac tissue can distinguish arrhythmic sudden death from coronary disease, providing molecular evidence in equivocal cases.

The History of Medicine as a formal academic discipline was pioneered by Henry Sigerist at Johns Hopkins, who argued that understanding disease requires social, economic, and cultural context; his students include Milton Terris and George Rosen, who founded modern social medicine and public health history.

source.name: Bulletin of the History of Medicine

text: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols — multimodal evidence-based bundles combining pre-operative carbohydrate loading, regional anesthesia, minimization of opioids, early mobilization, and early feeding — have reduced colorectal surgery hospital stay from 7–10 days to 3–4 days with no increase in complications.

The concept of 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence' is central to EBM: a Cochrane Review that finds no statistically significant effect does not prove an intervention is ineffective, but rather that available trials were insufficiently powered — an important distinction for clinical decision-making.

Mobile health (mHealth) interventions using SMS text messaging for medication adherence reminders have proven efficacy in HIV antiretroviral therapy in sub-Saharan Africa: a Cochrane Review found text messaging doubled treatment adherence compared to standard care, with viral suppression rates improving accordingly.

Mycetoma (Madura foot), a progressive destructive infection of skin, soft tissue, and bone caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or bacteria (actinomycetoma), is a neglected tropical disease affecting barefoot workers in Sudan, Mexico, and India; eumycetoma requires 12–24 months of antifungal treatment and still necessitates amputation in ~25% of cases.

Special Operations Combat Medics (18D in the US Army) receive the equivalent of a physician assistant education compressed into ~18 months, enabling them to provide advanced trauma care, emergency medicine, minor surgery, and even veterinary support in isolated environments — considered the most highly trained enlisted medical personnel in the US military.

Telemedicine for chronic wound management using smartphone photographs allows wound care nurses at spoke sites to consult remotely with wound care specialists; structured wound measurement apps that calculate wound area and track healing trajectories have shown to reduce healing time and unnecessary surgical consultations.

Cardiovascular deconditioning in space causes the heart to become more spherical (less elliptical) and reduces plasma volume by 10–15%; without countermeasures, returning astronauts experience orthostatic hypotension — difficulty standing without fainting — that requires adaptation protocols during Earth re-entry.

source.name: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

text: Forensic linguistics analyzes the language of ransom notes, threatening letters, suicide notes, and digital communications to assist criminal investigations; authorship attribution techniques use stylometric features (word frequency, sentence length, function word patterns) to identify or exclude suspect authors.

source.name: International Journal of Speech, Language and the Law

text: Disability studies as an interdisciplinary field within medical humanities challenges the 'medical model' — which frames disability as a deficit to be cured — in favor of the 'social model,' which locates the problem in environmental and social barriers; its insights have reformed rehabilitation medicine, architecture, and healthcare policy.

Ex-vivo machine perfusion of donor livers — keeping the organ warm and oxygenated on a circuit outside the body during transport and reconditioning — allows surgeons to assess viability and even treat marginal livers before transplanting, dramatically expanding the usable donor pool beyond what static cold storage permits.

Pragmatic clinical trials — designed to test interventions under real-world conditions with broad eligibility criteria, flexible dosing, and routine care comparators — provide more generalizable evidence than explanatory RCTs; the RECOVERY trial for COVID-19 exemplified this design, enrolling 40,000+ patients and identifying dexamethasone as life-saving within months.

Retinal telemedicine for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) screening in neonatal ICUs uses wide-field retinal cameras operated by nurses to image premature infants' retinas, with images transmitted for remote interpretation by ophthalmologists; this approach has dramatically increased the proportion of at-risk infants screened in underserved areas.

Loiasis, caused by the eye worm Loa loa and transmitted by Chrysops deer flies in the rainforests of Central and West Africa, manifests as the dramatic subconjunctival migration of adult worms across the eye; it complicates ivermectin mass drug administration programs because high Loa microfilaremia can cause fatal encephalopathy after treatment.

Tactical field care (the second phase of TCCC) occurs when the casualty and medic are not under direct fire; it prioritizes airway management, needle thoracostomy for tension pneumothorax, wound packing with hemostatic gauze, and intraosseous vascular access — all skills taught to every US military service member, not just medics.

Space medicine telemedicine uses real-time or time-delayed links between ISS crew and flight surgeons on the ground; astronauts are trained to perform emergency procedures including ultrasound, venipuncture, urinary catheterization, dental procedures, and even improvised surgical drainage under remote physician guidance.

Forensic document examination analyzes handwriting, paper, ink, and printing characteristics to authenticate or detect forgeries; the FBI Laboratory's questioned documents unit uses techniques including infrared reflectance, scanning electron microscopy, and ESDA (electrostatic detection apparatus) for indented writing.

Palliative medicine, recognized as a WHO-endorsed specialty since 2015, is fundamentally rooted in humanistic principles; Cicely Saunders, who founded the modern hospice movement and St Christopher's Hospice in London (1967), drew explicitly on narrative medicine — asking patients 'What is your pain like?' and listening to their stories to shape holistic care.

Colorectal surgery has been transformed by the total mesorectal excision (TME) technique, introduced by Bill Heald in 1982 — sharply dissecting along embryological fascial planes to remove the rectum with its intact mesorectal envelope — reducing local recurrence of rectal cancer from ~30% to below 5%.

Adaptive trial designs, such as response-adaptive randomization and seamless Phase II/III trials, allow modifications to sample size, treatment arms, or randomization ratios based on interim data without compromising type I error control; the FDA's 2019 guidance on adaptive designs has accelerated their uptake in drug development.

Virtual reality (VR) simulation for surgical training allows trainees to perform unlimited repetitions on photorealistic digital anatomies; studies of VR laparoscopic training show improvements in OR performance metrics including operative time, error rate, and economy of movement that transfer to live patient surgery.

The Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) model of delivering emergency surgical care in conflict zones — treating war wounds, obstetric emergencies, and epidemic diseases — has pushed evidence generation in resource-limited trauma surgery, documenting that context-adapted protocols can deliver life-saving outcomes without high-technology infrastructure.

Cysticercosis, the larval form of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm), causes neurocysticercosis when larvae encyst in the brain — the leading cause of preventable epilepsy in low-income countries, affecting ~50 million people; the disease is transmissible only through fecal-oral contact with human carriers, making improved sanitation and pork inspection the primary prevention strategies.

Prolonged field care (PFC) is an emerging military medical doctrine for Special Operations environments where MEDEVAC may be delayed 24–72+ hours; medics perform advanced interventions including blood transfusion, mechanical ventilation, point-of-care laboratory testing, and telemedicine consultation in austere locations.

Artificial gravity via centrifugation is a theorized long-duration spaceflight countermeasure; rotating a spacecraft or crew habitat to generate centrifugal force equivalent to partial Earth gravity could mitigate bone loss, muscle atrophy, and cardiovascular deconditioning simultaneously — but engineering, cost, and human tolerance constraints have prevented implementation.

Postmortem CT angiography (PMCTA) injects contrast medium into the vascular system of the deceased to visualize coronary arteries, aortic dissections, and pulmonary emboli with high accuracy, enabling determination of cardiovascular cause of death non-invasively in cases where traditional autopsy is culturally or religiously problematic.

The 'empathy map' and structured communication tools like SPIKES (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy) for breaking bad news were developed in the 1990s to give physicians a reproducible framework for one of medicine's most demanding tasks; randomized trials show SPIKES training significantly improves patient satisfaction and reduces physician distress.

Thoracoscopic surgery (VATS — Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery) for lung cancer lobectomy, first described in 1991, offers equivalent oncological outcomes to open thoracotomy with significantly less pain, shorter hospital stay, fewer complications, and faster return to chemotherapy — making it now the preferred approach at thoracic surgery centers.

source.name: Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery

text: Network meta-analysis (NMA) simultaneously compares multiple competing treatments across a network of trials — even those never directly compared head-to-head — using Bayesian or frequentist methods; Cochrane NMAs have generated treatment hierarchies for antidepressants, antihypertensives, and biologics in rheumatoid arthritis, directly guiding clinical guidelines.

mHealth solutions for surgical follow-up allow patients to report wound healing status via structured questionnaires and photographs after discharge; post-operative follow-up via app has been shown to detect surgical site infections earlier, reduce unnecessary clinic visits by 40%, and improve patient-reported satisfaction.

Chromoblastomycosis, a chronic cutaneous fungal infection caused by melanized ('black') fungi including Fonsecaea pedrosoi, affects barefoot agricultural workers in tropical regions; lesions grow over years into warty, cauliflower-like plaques that are notoriously difficult to treat and often recur even after years of antifungal therapy.

Close-quarters battle (CQB) medicine addresses the unique wounding patterns of urban warfare — multiple simultaneous penetrating wounds, blast injuries, and burns — requiring medics to rapidly triage, hemorrhage-control, and move multiple casualties under fire; the transition from individual to mass-casualty protocols is trained through immersive simulation exercises.

Telemedicine during the COVID-19 pandemic revealed significant digital equity gaps: patients without smartphones, reliable internet, or digital literacy — disproportionately elderly, low-income, and rural — were least able to access telehealth visits, raising concerns about amplifying existing health disparities if telemedicine replaces rather than supplements in-person care.

Cisplatin, first synthesized accidentally by Barnett Rosenberg in 1965 when platinum electrodes used in electrical current experiments inhibited E. coli cell division, became one of the most important chemotherapy drugs in history — now curative for >95% of testicular cancers and used widely in ovarian, bladder, and head-and-neck cancers.

The 'narrative competence' framework proposed by Rita Charon identifies five skills — attention, representation, affiliation, interpretation, and reflection — as core competencies for physician readers of patient stories; these are now assessed in Columbia's Master of Science in Narrative Medicine program through close reading exercises with literary texts.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is the only common hematological indication for splenectomy in adults; removing the spleen eliminates the primary site of anti-platelet antibody production and platelet sequestration, achieving durable remission in ~60% of cases — though biologics like romiplostim and eltrombopag have made surgery less frequent.

The Cochrane Library's plain language summaries translate technical systematic review findings into accessible prose for patients and the public — recognizing that informed patient decision-making requires comprehensible evidence; versions in over 14 languages make EBM findings globally accessible.

Global obstetric surgery access remains gravely inequitable: 99% of the 300,000 maternal deaths annually occur in low- and middle-income countries where caesarean section rates are critically below the minimum 5–10% threshold WHO recommends; strengthening surgical capacity is inseparable from achieving maternal health targets.

Clonorchiasis and opisthorchiasis — liver fluke infections acquired through eating raw freshwater fish — are leading risk factors for cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer) in Southeast Asia; Opisthorchis viverrini infects ~10 million people in Laos, Thailand, and Cambodia, and the Mekong River basin has the world's highest cholangiocarcinoma incidence.

The NATO Trauma Registry and the North Atlantic Surgical Trauma Research Collaboration compare outcomes across Alliance nations' military hospitals, enabling identification of best practices in damage control resuscitation, blood product ratios, and early definitive surgery that would be impossible in any single nation's combat experience.

source.name: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

text: Crew medical officers on long-duration spaceflight may face scenarios requiring improvised procedures without specialist support; a study of ISS medical events over 20 years found 26% of significant medical issues were musculoskeletal, 17% skin-related, and 7% dental — most successfully managed aboard with remote ground support.

Sexual assault forensic examination (SAFE) uses specialized kits — 'rape kits' — to collect DNA evidence, document injuries, and preserve chain of custody; the backlog of untested kits in US jurisdictions exceeded 200,000 in 2017, prompting federal funding for processing that has led to thousands of prosecutions and exonerations.

Medical clowning — the use of trained therapeutic clown artists in pediatric wards — has been shown in randomized trials to reduce preoperative anxiety in children more effectively than midazolam sedation, and to lower pain scores and stress biomarkers during procedures such as IV placement and wound dressing changes.

Three-dimensional printing of patient-specific anatomical models for surgical planning — generated from CT/MRI DICOM data — allows surgeons to rehearse complex reconstructions of facial trauma, pelvic fractures, or congenital heart defects before the actual procedure, with studies demonstrating shorter operative time and fewer complications.

Surrogate endpoints — biomarkers like CD4 count, viral load, or HbA1c — are used in clinical trials to substitute for harder-to-measure outcomes like mortality or disability; EBM emphasizes that surrogate endpoints can mislead when their link to true outcomes is uncertain, as demonstrated by the harmful CAST trial (antiarrhythmic drugs that reduced arrhythmias but increased deaths).

Anesthesia mortality has fallen over 50 years from approximately 1 death per 1,500 procedures to 1 per 100,000–200,000 in high-income countries — driven by pulse oximetry, capnography, standardized checklists, improved pharmacology, and simulation-based training, making anesthesia one of the greatest patient safety success stories in modern medicine.

Telehealth for home-based cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction, evaluated in multiple Cochrane-reviewed trials, achieves equivalent improvement in exercise capacity, cardiovascular risk factors, and quality of life compared to centre-based rehabilitation — with significantly higher uptake rates, removing geographical and logistical barriers to participation.

Podoconiosis, non-filarial elephantiasis caused by long-term barefoot exposure to volcanic red clay soil containing fine silica particles that trigger lymphatic inflammation, affects ~4 million people in highland areas of Ethiopia, Cameroon, and Uganda; it is entirely preventable by wearing shoes and washing feet — yet receives virtually no global funding.

Emergency wartime blood transfusion was pioneered in WWI by Oswald Robertson of the US Army Medical Corps, who developed the first blood bank by collecting, citrating, and refrigerating O-negative blood near the front; his work established that blood could be stored and delivered to multiple casualties — a practice saving millions of lives to this day.

Telepsychology for PTSD using prolonged exposure therapy delivered via video demonstrated in a landmark VA-funded randomized trial non-inferiority to in-person treatment for veterans — with lower dropout rates in the telehealth arm — making effective trauma-focused psychotherapy accessible to rural and mobility-impaired veterans.

Surgical site infection (SSI) is the most common healthcare-associated infection after surgery, affecting 2–5% of patients and costing the US healthcare system over $3.5 billion annually; WHO's 29 SSI prevention recommendations include skin preparation, antibiotic prophylaxis timing, normothermia, and evidence-based glycemic control.

Trachoma surgery — entropion correction using the WHO-recommended BLTR (bilamellar tarsal rotation) procedure — can be performed in 15 minutes by trained ophthalmic nurses in village settings, preventing the blinding scarring cycle; over 200,000 surgeries have been performed annually as part of the global trachoma elimination program.

Histopathology simulation using whole slide imaging (digital pathology) allows trainees to examine virtual glass slides on screens, practice pattern recognition, and receive immediate AI-generated feedback; studies in hematopathology, dermatopathology, and renal pathology show digital teaching is equivalent to glass slide training.

source.name: Archives of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine

text: Medical ethics consultation services, staffed by interdisciplinary teams including physicians, nurses, social workers, clergy, and ethicists, handle conflicts over end-of-life care, medical futility, surrogate decision-making, and resource allocation; they have become standard in US hospitals since the Joint Commission began requiring ethics mechanisms in 1992.

Extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacteriaceae — a global surgical and tropical medicine crisis — are prevalent in community settings across South Asia, Southeast Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, meaning patients from these regions undergoing surgery are at high risk for surgical site infections with organisms resistant to standard prophylactic antibiotics.

Closed-loop anesthesia drug delivery systems that automatically adjust propofol infusion rates using bispectral index (BIS) feedback have been validated in trials to maintain target depth of anesthesia more precisely than manual dosing, reducing drug consumption by ~20% and speeding recovery times.

The number of Cochrane Reviews using individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis — pooling raw data from all trials rather than aggregate summary statistics — has grown substantially; IPD meta-analysis is considered the 'platinum standard' and allows subgroup analyses impossible with published summary data, for example identifying which cancer patients benefit most from specific chemotherapy regimens.

Leishmaniasis Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) — a skin eruption that follows visceral leishmaniasis treatment in ~5–10% of South Asian and up to 50–60% of East African patients — is an important transmission reservoir; understanding and treating PKDL is essential to WHO's visceral leishmaniasis elimination programs.

The SOFTT-W (Special Operations Forces Tactical Tourniquet-Wide) and CAT (Combat Application Tourniquet) are the two tourniquets proven most effective in combat-use data from Afghanistan and Iraq; the CAT alone is credited with preventing an estimated 2,000 deaths from extremity hemorrhage in those conflicts.

Psychological impact of deep space isolation was studied in the Mars-500 mission simulation (520-day lockdown at Moscow's IBMP, 2010–2011), where crew members experienced progressive reduction in physical activity, disrupted sleep, and mild depressive symptoms — findings informing behavioral health countermeasures for actual Mars missions.

Forensic nursing, a specialty recognized by the American Nurses Association in 1995, integrates nursing care with forensic science in cases of sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, and death investigation; Sexual Assault Nurse Examiners (SANEs) have been shown to improve evidentiary quality and patient-centered care compared to physician-led examinations.

The 'Teaching Kitchen' movement, pioneered at Harvard Medical School's Teaching Kitchen Collaborative, incorporates culinary education into medical training and community health programs; physicians who understand cooking and nutrition as lived practices demonstrate significantly improved ability to counsel patients on dietary change.

Liver transplantation for hepatocellular carcinoma is governed by the Milan criteria (1 tumor ≤5 cm or 3 tumors each ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion, no extrahepatic disease) proposed by Mazzaferro in 1996; patients within Milan criteria have 5-year survival exceeding 70%, and expanded criteria are being validated at leading transplant centers.

Competency-based medical education (CBME), replacing time-based training with milestone assessment, was mandated for US internal medicine residencies in 2013 through the ACGME Next Accreditation System; residents progress through defined stages of entrustable professional activities (EPAs), assessed by direct observation rather than hours-logged.

Neglected tropical disease drug discovery is largely driven by the Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative (DNDi), a non-profit founded in 2003 with MSF; it has delivered 9 new treatments — including fexinidazole for sleeping sickness, ASAQ for malaria, and nifurtimox-eflornithine for late-stage HAT — at a fraction of the cost of traditional pharmaceutical R&D.

Telemedicine in low-resource settings is enabled by global health organizations like Partners in Health, which has deployed teleradiology and teleconsultation platforms in Haiti, Rwanda, and Liberia — where a single smartphone with satellite internet allows community health workers to escalate complex cases to specialist physicians at partner academic medical centers.

Wearable exoskeletons for surgical assistance — robotic vests that support the surgeon's arms during prolonged laparoscopic or robotic operations — have been tested in multicenter trials and shown to reduce muscle fatigue, tremor, and ergonomic injury risk in surgeons performing operations lasting more than 4 hours.

Open Payments (the US Sunshine Act, implemented 2013) requires pharmaceutical and device companies to publicly disclose all transfers of value to physicians; analyses of the database reveal that even small industry payments — meals under $20 — are associated with higher prescribing of sponsor brands, raising EBM concerns about conflicts of interest in clinical guidelines.

Astronaut Scott Kelly's year-long ISS mission demonstrated reversible telomere lengthening during spaceflight followed by rapid attrition post-return — a paradox possibly explained by reduced oxidative stress in microgravity combined with post-flight inflammatory rebound — with long-term implications for cancer risk monitoring in career astronauts.

Death certification accuracy is a fundamental forensic medicine concern: studies show that primary care physicians correctly identify the underlying cause of death in only 50–70% of cases compared with autopsy findings — a systematic error with major consequences for vital statistics, public health resource allocation, and research.

Balint groups — small reflective discussion groups where clinicians present and analyze difficult patient encounters — were developed by psychoanalyst Michael Balint at the Tavistock Clinic in 1950s London and are now used in medical training globally as a tool for improving clinician self-awareness and preventing burnout.

Indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence imaging, used during laparoscopic and robotic surgery, allows real-time visualization of bile ducts, tissue perfusion, and sentinel lymph nodes by injecting ICG and using a near-infrared camera; ICG cholangiography has reduced bile duct injuries during cholecystectomy by enabling surgeons to see the biliary anatomy before cutting.

Pragmatic evidence synthesis using real-world data (RWD) — claims databases, electronic health records, patient registries — complements randomized trial evidence in EBM; the FDA's Real-World Evidence program has approved two drugs based partly on RWD and is developing frameworks for when RWD can substitute for RCTs in regulatory decisions.

Leishmaniasis vaccine development has been hampered by the parasite's complex immune evasion strategies; the first human Leishmania vaccine (LEISH-F3 + GLA-SE adjuvant) has reached Phase 2 trials, and killed whole-parasite vaccines such as Leishvacin showed partial efficacy in Brazil — but as of 2024, no licensed vaccine exists for human leishmaniasis.

Simulation in obstetric emergencies using high-fidelity birthing mannequins has become standard training for managing shoulder dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage, and eclampsia; multidisciplinary team simulation drills at hospitals have been linked to significant reductions in brachial plexus injuries and neonatal hypoxic injury in multiple health systems.

source.name: BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology

text: Military burn care was transformed during the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan: the US Army Institute of Surgical Research at San Antonio became the world's most experienced burn center, developing the 'Rule of Ten' simplified resuscitation formula and demonstrating that early excision and grafting of burn wounds reduces mortality in blast-injury patients.

source.name: Journal of Burn Care and Research

text: The Cochrane Neonatal Group has produced over 600 reviews covering premature birth interventions; one of its most influential, confirming antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation, synthesized evidence showing betamethasone given to mothers in preterm labor reduces neonatal respiratory distress syndrome by 34% — a standard of care since 1994.

Teledentistry using asynchronous photographs of teeth and oral cavities allows dentists to triage dental pain, spot caries, and provide interim prescriptions, particularly valuable in correctional facilities and rural communities without dentists; rural Australia's School Dental Service has used telehealth screening since 2012.

Praziquantel, the drug of choice for all human schistosomiasis and most tapeworm infections, was discovered in a joint effort between Bayer and Merck KGaA in 1972 and licensed in 1979; despite being on WHO's Essential Medicines List, patent expiry and the Merck KGaA donation program are required to make it affordable in the countries that most need it.

Narrative oncology programs, embedded in cancer centers at Memorial Sloan Kettering and MD Anderson, offer patients structured journaling, creative writing workshops, and storytelling sessions; randomized trials show these interventions reduce anxiety, improve coping, and enhance sense of personal identity beyond the cancer diagnosis.
